text: 9:05 a.m. The boss is at your desk, tapping his watch. You were on time — his watch is just ten minutes fast. Show him your phone?
left: Show him the time on your phone

text: The team lead moves stand-up to 8:30 “while our heads are fresh.” His head is fresh. Yours is still asleep. Push back?
The deputy director tours the office with a tablet: “What exactly are you working on right now?” You’re pouring tea. What do you say?
You got added to the management chat by mistake. They’re discussing who to “optimize” this spring. Nobody’s noticed you yet. Keep reading?
The boss declares a “quiet hour” from 10 to 11. He spends the whole hour on speakerphone. Remind him of the rule?
left: Put a sign on his desk

text: The CEO mistakes you for a courier and hands you an envelope: “To the tax office, urgent!” He’s already at the elevator. Chase him down?
The boss sent an 11-minute voice message. It starts with: “Real quick.” Listen to all of it or ask for text?
On day two, the new VP of Development announces he’s going to “rebuild everything here.” Ask what exactly?
Your manager wants you in half an hour early “to clear email before the morning meeting.” Leaving early isn’t on the table. Agree?
The boss demanded the deck by 3:00. At 2:55 you learn the meeting was moved this morning — and he knew. Say something?
The team lead left 47 comments on your memo. Thirty are about commas. Fix them all?
At the all-hands, the CEO quotes revenue off by a factor of ten. You know the right number. Correct him?
left: Raise your hand and correct him

text: The deputy and your manager gave you opposite orders. Both urgent, both “approved upstairs.” Who wins?
right: Loop them both into one email

text: For the fifth time this month, the boss asks how to make a pivot table. His eyes are so sincere. Show him again?
7:00 p.m. The boss calls from a cab: “You live near me, right? Check if I left the iron on.” His keys are on your desk. Go?
10:40 p.m. The CEO posts in the company chat: “Anyone still up — share ideas for growing sales.” You are up. Admit it?
8:15 p.m. The team lead drops a funny deadline meme in chat, captioned: “By the way, deadline’s tomorrow.” Your move?
left: Like it and go to bed

text: The CEO’s assistant: “Leadership expects you in a meeting in ten minutes. Topic undisclosed.” What do you do?
The boss invites you to his three-hour client meeting. Your role: “look smart.” You have a mountain of tasks today. Go?
The department head launches “Employee of the Month.” He’s the only voter. Prize: the parking spot by the door. Compete?
Annual review: “Meets expectations.” Asked “whose?”, the boss says: “Well, mine.” It’s 5:40 p.m., everyone’s leaving. Dispute it?
New policy: emails to management must open with “Dear colleague, allow me to bring to your attention.” Even an email saying “OK.” Comply?
Reorg: your department was renamed three times this week. The sign on the door is two versions behind. Now what?
In the evening, the boss sends a photo of the meeting whiteboard: “Digitize by morning.” Handwriting like a doctor after a night shift. Take it on?
right: Ask for help in the morning

text: The team lead books an 8:45 “1:1, let’s talk about growth.” The description is empty. Cause for alarm?
The CFO wants your department budget cut 20% “so nobody notices.” Proposals due by 4:00. What gets cut?
The boss asks you to check his social media post. “Efficiency” appears nine times in three lines. Tell him?
6:30 p.m. The CEO’s assistant asks for help with a board report “for like an hour.” Their hours run long. Stay?
The boss walks in wearing a loud new shirt, clearly waiting for a reaction. The whole team pretends to be very busy. Compliment it?
New order: lunch strictly from 1:00 to 1:30. The cafeteria line at 1:00 is forty minutes long. How do you eat?
right: Eat a sandwich at your desk

text: The CEO holds an “open mic” — anyone can ask anything. The silence has lasted a full minute. Everyone’s looking at you. Ask?
right: Ask about plans for the year

text: 5:58 p.m. Your manager asks for a “tiny edit” to a contract. It touches all 40 pages. Do it today?
A meeting called “Conversation” with your manager and HR appears in your calendar. 15 minutes. Nothing else. Brace for the worst?
left: Update your résumé, just in case

text: Your manager offers to make you the interns’ mentor. No extra pay, but “with prospects.” Which prospects, he doesn’t say. Agree?
The team lead asks you to estimate a task in story points. You say eight. He says: “Let’s say three.” Agree?
At the evening reception, the CEO asks your name for the third time this year — and promises to remember it. Answer?
8:50 a.m. Boss: “Stop by before the meeting.” A minute later: “Nothing bad.” A minute after that: “Probably.” Go?
You’re called to the board meeting to “answer a couple technical questions.” They ask about what the department next door does. Now what?
Your manager went on vacation without naming a backup. Nobody can sign an urgent document. Sign for him?
Friday, 6:10 p.m. Boss, in his jacket with briefcase and keys in hand: “I’m out, but message me if anything comes up.” Will you?
A “Rate Your Manager” survey arrives. Anonymous, they promise. Oddly, the link contains your employee ID. Fill it out?
The CEO decides to test the new CRM himself and calls you: “Where’s the ‘Make It Good’ button?” Explain?
left: Explain by phone for an hour
right: Send a link to the manual

text: The boss wanted the report as a PDF, then Word, then “normal, in a spreadsheet.” Now he wants a PDF. Where’s the line?
The team lead throws an evening release “code-a-thon.” Pizza’s on him, but it runs till 11 p.m. Stay?
The department head shows up Monday with a book: “Leadership in Seven Days.” Today’s day one. Chapter: “Radical Candor.” Be afraid?
The CEO’s assistant needs someone who “speaks English” to greet a delegation. You once said “yes” in an elevator. Your big chance?
The boss asks you to “just think about” the budget over the weekend. On Monday he’ll want to see what you came up with. Start thinking now?
left: Give your evening to the budget

text: New rule from above: vacations must be approved six months ahead. Yours is in a month, tickets bought. What now?
In front of the whole team, the boss asks why the task isn’t done. He assigned it forty minutes ago. Verbally. Your answer?
7:20 p.m. The deputy director texts: “Awake? It’s not about work.” The next message is a work file. Open it?
left: Open it and take a look

text: The boss opens the morning meeting: “Two pieces of news — good and work.” Good: cake on Friday. Work: audit on Saturday. Your reaction?
left: Cheer for the cake out loud

text: The CEO published the company mission. Fourteen points, not a single verb. You’re asked to hang it in every office. Do it?
left: Hang them with a straight face
right: Hang one by the coffee machine

text: The team lead set up a task board: “To Do,” “Doing,” “Discuss with Team Lead.” The third column already has 40 cards. Remind him?
At 8:12 a.m. your manager emails with the subject “!!!”. One line inside: “Let’s discuss.” No attachments. Investigate before the meeting?
The deputy CEO wants to “be closer to the people” and moves into the open space for a day. Right at the desk next to yours. How do you work?
The boss asks you to “quietly” find out who on the team is job hunting. He “just wants to understand.” Take the spy job?
Management announced a “no-meetings week.” Three meetings have been scheduled to plan it. Attend them all?
right: Skip them to get work done

text: CEO: “Need someone for an interview with the city news site, urgently.” Topic: “How we take care of our people.” You’ve stayed late three days running. Go?
The team lead asks you to run the retro for him because he’s “not emotionally ready.” The whole team is mad at him specifically. Run it?
The department head fines latecomers to the meeting $5 into a team jar. He’s late every single day. Mention the jar?
left: Put the jar on his desk

text: 6:20 p.m. The boss says, “You can go, I’m not keeping you.” And doesn’t take his eyes off you. Leave?
In his evening blog post, the CEO explains how he “built our processes.” You built them. Your name isn’t mentioned. Comment?
9:00 p.m. Team lead: “Sorry for the late hour, two-second question.” The question requires digging through three years of archives. Answer?
The CFO rejects your travel expense report: the cab receipt doesn’t state the “purpose of the trip.” Redo it?
Back from a conference, the boss wants five “best practices” at once. One is standing desks, another is lying-down meetings. Support him?
right: Ask to roll out one at a time

text: The sales director promised a client something your product can’t do. The client calls you asking where the feature is. What do you say?
The boss wants a “quick” brief for the CEO. An hour later he adds charts. Another hour — a five-year forecast. Stop him?
left: Ask where the finish line is

text: Your manager left a printout of the team’s salaries in the meeting room. You found it first. What do you do?
5:30 p.m. The leadership meeting enters its third hour. CEO: “Let’s do one last item.” Nine items remain on the agenda. Leave?
right: Sit it out to the end

text: The boss wants you to replace him on an industry panel tomorrow. Topic: “Digital Transformation.” You find out at 8:30 p.m. Agree?
The new director asks everyone to submit an “essay on your value.” Two pages minimum. Due today at noon. Write it?
The department head holds a 9:00 a.m. Monday meeting to discuss the results of Friday’s meeting. You don’t remember Friday. Now what?
The CEO decides to personally greet staff at the turnstile and log arrival times. It’s 9:04. Walk past him?
The boss messages: “Can you talk?” You reply “Yes.” Then an hour and a half of silence. Wait for the call?
The deputy manager pitches your idea at the meeting as his own. The manager praises him. Step in?
HR partner: you’ve been nominated for promotion. You just need six interviews with leadership this week. Start?
right: Ask to cut it to two

text: At the evening party, the CEO dances alone in the middle of the room and waves at you. Coworkers look away. Join him?
Friday evening. The boss sent an email titled “Important changes starting Monday” and turned off his phone. Open it now?
The team lead wants a daily “productivity journal” in 15-minute blocks. Your first entry: “9:00–9:15 — filled out journal.” Send it?
Your manager asks you to write your own reference for a promotion by lunch. In his name, but about you. How hard to brag?
New policy: every purchase over $100 needs management approval. You need a $120 toner cartridge. How do you handle it?
The CEO is showing everyone photos of his new puppy. Now it’s your turn — but you’re on a client call. What do you do?
The boss signed you up for “Effective Communication” training. Asked why, he says: “Well, you know.” Go?
6:45 p.m. The department head remembers the quarterly report is due upstairs today. Nobody’s started it. Save the day?
The CEO’s assistant invites you to an “informal meeting with leadership” at the bowling alley, 8 p.m. Attendance “encouraged.” Go?
The boss wants a draft of every client email sent to him for approval first. You send forty a day. Agree?
right: Offer to clear the key ones

text: The CEO sent everyone a 23-minute audio greeting for the company anniversary. Rumor says bonuses are announced at the end. Listen to it all?
The team lead asks you to review code from an intern he hired himself. The code clearly runs on luck. How do you phrase feedback?
For the first time in a year, your manager praises you in a meeting. You suspect a new assignment is coming. Be on guard?
The boss’s laptop is dying right before his presentation to the CEO. Only your charger fits. Your laptop is also at zero. Hand it over?
9:00 p.m. The CEO messages you directly: “How do you feel about moving to another office?” No other context. Reply?
The team lead files tasks at 11 p.m. so everyone “wakes up with clarity.” You wake up with anxiety. Ask him to file them during the day?
The deputy boss brings a cake for his own birthday and opens the meeting by asking who hasn’t congratulated him yet. Be first?
The department head sent a “Your Goals for the Year” form. Question three: “Where do you see yourself in five years?” Be honest?
Management bans eating at your desk. An hour later, the CEO strolls through the office holding a shawarma. Bring it up?
The boss wants you to send an email “under your name, but like it’s from me.” The recipient is his boss. Whose signature?
The CEO holds a meeting right in the cafeteria, “like a startup.” You’re stuck with a full tray between him and the exit. What now?
Evening. Boss: “On a scale of one to ten, how would you rate your work this year?” It’s a trick question. What number?
7:10 p.m. Your manager asks you to call the client in his place and report a missed deadline. He missed it. Call?
You’re invited to dinner with the board. Beforehand the CEO whispers: “Don’t mention the delays.” They ask about exactly that. What do you say?
The boss assigns you a task through the glass wall of the meeting room, by gesture. He draws a square in the air and holds up five fingers. Meaning?
CEO’s decree: everyone wears logo T-shirts on Friday. The shirts handed out are three sizes too big. Wear one?
left: Wear it, tied in a knot

text: The team lead brings a timer to stand-up and mutes anyone who talks over a minute. He doesn’t time himself. Point it out?
The department head says he “dreamed up” a new report last night. The idea sounds like a sci-fi movie plot. Your reaction?
right: Ask him to wake up first

text: The deputy CEO demands fewer calls and “more in writing.” A minute later, he calls you to discuss it. Pick up?
The boss holds a post-mortem on a project everyone agreed was a success. He wants to know how it could’ve been “even more successful.” Offer something?
The CEO dropped by to borrow a pen and stayed to discuss exchange rates. You’re due on a call in five minutes. Interrupt?
Management is moving every department to another floor. Your desk goes by the window, your team by the elevator. Ask to go with them?
After the meeting, the team lead whispers: “Just between us — who do you think is our weak link?” Nobody else around. Your answer?
Your manager canceled your client meeting so you could help him pick a new office chair. He’s been on the chair for three hours. Put up with it?
5:45 p.m. The boss walks in with a soda: “So, stay a bit late? Celebrate the quarter with some work!” Sounds like an invitation. Accept?
At the meeting, the CEO asks who’s ready to “lead a new initiative.” Your hand went up on its own — you were stretching. Confess?
The deputy CEO invites you to a Friday dinner, “inner circle only.” You’re the only rank-and-file employee on the list. People are whispering. Go?
The CFO cut office supplies: pens are now signed out, one per quarter. Someone at the meeting stole yours. What now?
The boss asks for “yesterday’s” report. You didn’t send one yesterday, and he never asked. Admit it or play along?
right: Whip one up in an hour

text: The department head offers to move you to an “aggressively growing” unit. Rumor is only turnover grows aggressively there. Accept?
At the meeting, the CEO writes “SYNERGIE” on the flip chart. Everyone’s silent. You’re holding the marker. Fix it?
The boss wants you to write his answer to an “awkward question” from the CEO. The CEO hasn’t asked anything yet. Write it?
The team lead holds a “laptop-free hour”: ideas on sticky notes only. Half an hour in, the sticky notes run out but the ideas don’t. Now what?
6:30 p.m. Your manager invites you to a “chat about the future.” Turns out the future is tomorrow at 7 a.m., at a job site. Agree?
The CEO’s assistant tells you in secret: you were discussed at the board meeting. No details, but “the boss had a weird look.” Worry?
Management made Monday “five-minute check-ins” mandatory. The first lasted 70 minutes. The second is at 8:30. Arrive early?
The boss sends a link to “10 Habits of Successful Employees,” with: “Might come in handy.” You counted twelve habits. Reply?
The CEO’s assistant is rounding up “volunteers” for a Saturday cleanup day. Your name is already on the list, with a check mark. Cross it off?
The CEO came to your talk, sat in the front row, and fell asleep on slide three. He’s starting to snore. How do you go on?
The department head delegates you a task the deputy delegated to him, which the CEO delegated to the deputy. Along the way, a week shrank to tonight. Take it?
Evening. The boss sends “send me that contact, pls,” then deletes the message. It already came through. Send it?
10:00 p.m. Team lead: “Don’t reply, this is for tomorrow.” Five minutes later: “Although if you’re up…” You’re up. Reply?
The CEO sent everyone a “Letter from the Future” where the company is market leader in five years. He wants letters back. Write one?
The deputy manager runs a “quick policy knowledge check.” Question one: the section number of the dress code rule. Answer?
The boss asks you to “google a competitor.” Turns out the competitor is his ex-coworker and the interest is personal. Keep going?
Presenting to the CEO, your manager shows your slide with the typo “QUATERLY REPROT.” The CEO is already squinting. Speak up?
Management put an “Idea Box” in every office. Only the cleaner has the key. Drop an idea in?
Friday, 7:00 p.m. The CEO posts a video: “Thanks, everyone, for the week!” You were on vacation. Your manager wants a “response from the team.” Write it?
The department head hosts a “strategic board game night.” He invented the game; the rules run 80 pages. Starts at 7:30. Go?
The team lead hands out “competency maps” to mark what you can do. You hesitantly check “stays motivated.” Submit?
9:10 a.m. The boss walks in: “I have great news.” You flinch — last time the great news was a renovation mid-quarter. Listen?
The CEO is handing out certificates. He mispronounces your name and the room applauds a stranger. Correct him?
The deputy director wants you to sub for him at a meeting: “Nothing complicated, just sign.” You’d be signing the annual budget. Go?
The boss asks you to print an email he sent you so he can read it to you out loud. Is this normal?
right: Offer to read it on screen

text: 6:05 p.m. Manager: “Go, of course. Though I do wonder when you plan to finish the report.” Respond?
Management sent an engagement survey. Question: “How often do you stay late?” Options: “sometimes,” “often,” “always.” Your pick?
In the morning, the department head publicly thanks you for a “wonderful report.” The guy at the next desk wrote it. Speak up?
The CEO rules that the elevator only goes up now; down is “stairs, for your health.” You’re on the 12th floor. Comply?
The team lead wants you to “own communication with other departments.” Meaning: fight with Accounting on his behalf. Take it?
The boss wants you to pick a gift for the CEO’s milestone birthday, “within reason.” Budget: zero — the team chips in. Pass the hat?
right: Give a card from the team

text: Your manager shows off his new “priority organizer.” Under “Urgent and Important” — your name. Ask what that means?
The CEO invites everyone to his birthday at a restaurant — “everyone pays their own way.” One entrée costs your weekly budget. Go?
8:00 p.m. Deputy director: “Urgent, call me.” You call back — no answer. Third time this has happened. Keep waiting?
Late-night message from the boss: “Don’t be late tomorrow — there’ll be a surprise.” Last time the surprise was a snap inspection. How do you prepare?
Monday, the boss opens with: “I looked through your tasks over the weekend.” You didn’t know he had access to your tracker. Be wary?
The department head wants to “reboot the team”: everyone swaps tasks with their neighbor for a month. Yours runs warehouse bookkeeping. Agree?
The team lead introduced “Monday goals”: one goal per week. Yours, “survive till Friday,” failed moderation. Rewrite it?
The CEO rolls into the office on a scooter and urges everyone to commute “green.” That means leaving an hour earlier. Support it?
An email “To all managers” landed in your inbox by mistake. Subject: “Staffing chart changes.” Open it?
right: Forward it back to the sender

text: At lunch, the boss asks you to tag along to pick out a gift for his wife. You wanted to eat. Go?
right: Go, but eat on the way

text: Manager: “Do it however you think is best.” An hour later: “Why did you do it that way?” Explain yourself?
The CEO drops into the cafeteria and asks loudly: “So, who’ll tell me what’s wrong here?” Everyone stares at their plates. Speak up?
The deputy manager lost the flash drive with the CEO deck five minutes before the meeting. Your draft is the only copy. Hand it over?
New order: every employee reports weekly on their “contribution to company culture.” Yours: you brought cookies. Write that?
7:40 p.m. Boss: “Take a look at my LinkedIn post, please.” It’s about how he “grew the team.” Edit it?
Evening DM from the team lead: “I want to be frank. You’re a good specialist, but…” — and he vanishes. The “but” has hung there for an hour. Ask?
6:15 p.m. The CEO calls the whole department in “for five minutes.” The talk about leaving on time runs till 7:30. Object?
The department head declares an “open door day.” The door is open, but his assistant stands in front of it turning everyone away. Push through?
The boss wants a “short industry news digest” at 9:00 every morning. Today there’s no news. None. What do you send?
The CEO wants a “walking meeting” in the park. It’s pouring rain. He won’t cancel. Umbrella or doctor’s note?
The team lead wants your project presented “so leadership gets it.” Last time leadership fell asleep. What do you change?
Your manager hands you an “acknowledgment form” for a document he never showed you. Sign it?
The boss asks your opinion on the new team structure: “Be honest.” Last time, “honest” ended in a reprimand. Risk it?
The deputy CEO takes you to a bar after work and starts complaining about the CEO. You silently stir your lemonade. Join in?
5:50 p.m. The department head assigns the “last task of the week.” It’s the same task he canceled on Monday. Remind him?
The CEO posts a poem in the company chat to celebrate the quarter’s end. It rhymes “results” with “team exults.” React?
8:40 a.m. The CEO’s assistant calls: “The boss wants you to bring him coffee at the meeting, since you’re nearby.” You’re across town. Admit it?
Friday morning, the team lead hands out tasks: “Whoever grabs the hard one first gets to leave early.” The hard one is a week’s work. Take it?
Management swapped paper passes for key cards. Yours won’t open your manager’s office. He thinks you’re avoiding him. Explain?
The boss wants you to attend a partner’s office opening in his place and “cut the ribbon.” Bring your own scissors. Go?
The deputy manager rolls out a “personal accountability table.” Your column: “everything else.” Dispute it?
Your manager asks you to sit in on a meeting “just to fill seats.” At the meeting, it turns out you’re the presenter. What now?
The team lead schedules a video call at 8 p.m. for the team’s birthday. Cameras mandatory, cake optional. Join?
In the team chat, the boss writes: “Who’s been a star today?” You left at 5:00; everyone else is still there. Reply?
Morning email from the CEO: “Our goal is 300% growth.” The department head forwards it: “Let’s discuss how you’ll make that happen.” Prepare?
The department head arrives with a thermos and offers everyone an “invigorating brew.” It smells of hay and regret. Try it?
The boss runs a “task lottery”: draw a slip, get a project. Yours says “You know what.” Ask for details?
The CEO messages you by mistake: “Buy bread.” A minute later: “Not you.” Another minute: “But if you’re nearby…” Buy it?
HR partner says your manager filed a “positive complaint” about you: you work too much. Your reaction?
Leadership is discussing your project without inviting you. You overhear it through a thin wall. Walk in?
6:00 p.m. Manager: “Auditors arrive tomorrow. Act natural.” You’re trying to figure out what natural looks like. Prepare?
The deputy CEO sent an email marked “confidential” to 80 recipients. You’re one of them. Reply All?
The boss posts a “productivity ranking” on the hallway board. You’re second, behind someone on parental leave. Dispute it?
The CEO posts a photo of his morning run: “Who’s with me tomorrow at six?” Your department head has already liked it and tagged you. Run?
The team lead offers you a “lateral promotion”: same title, different project, same desk. Sounds very grand. Accept?
The department head vanished after lunch. An hour later the CEO is looking for him. You know he’s at the dentist. Tell?
The boss wants the report written “so the CEO doesn’t ask anything.” The CEO always asks. How do you write it?
right: Warn him: there will be questions

text: 6:30 p.m. The CEO hosts a “Q&A evening.” He asks the first question himself and answers it for 40 minutes. Ask the second?
Friday, 6:40 p.m. Boss: “Come see me first thing Monday, we need to talk.” No topic. Your weekend is in danger. Ask now?
New policy: all files must be named “YYYY_MM_DD_dept_author_version_status.” Your file is called “final2_for_real.” Rename?
Morning message from the team lead: “We work in silence today, my throat hurts.” An hour later he calls a voice meeting to croak out tasks. Join?
The CFO wants justification for a new mouse, including ROI. The mouse costs $8. Write it?
Your manager is late to his own client meeting and asks you to “stall.” The client is already checking his watch. How do you stall?
The boss wants you at a trade show this weekend, “just to walk around and look.” Then a ten-page report. Go?
7:50 a.m. Boss: “Are you in the office today?” You’re on sick leave — he signed the paperwork himself. Reply?
The CEO decides every meeting now opens with a minute of gratitude. You have to thank someone first. Who?
At the meeting, the department head reads your client email aloud as “an example of what not to do.” There are no mistakes in it. Push back?
left: Ask him to show the errors

text: The team lead asks you to fill out his self-review: “You know better what I did.” Praise him?
The CEO suddenly announces: “Short day today!” Ten minutes later his assistant clarifies: “For leadership.” Leave anyway?
At the meeting the boss says: “I asked you to do this last month!” Last month you hadn’t been hired yet. Remind him?
The deputy manager asks you to sign a card “from the whole team” for the manager. 19 signatures already, not a single wish. Write something?
A new KPI from above: “% of satisfied clients.” You’re assigned to survey them. The clients don’t respond. What now?
8:30 p.m. Manager: “Sorry for the late hour, but tomorrow you’re giving an hour-long talk.” First you’ve heard of it. Back out?
To save money, the CEO turned off the office lights at exactly 7:00 p.m. You’re in the dark, saving your file by feel. Go home?
The team lead introduced daily “emotional check-ins”: pick a mood emoji. Your actual mood isn’t on the list. What do you pick?
The boss came in sick and heroically stays “for the team.” He sneezes in your direction. Send him home?
The department head asks you to interview a candidate for a job above yours. Your future boss is more nervous than you. Help him out?
The CEO personally checks who’s on social media during work hours. You’re on social media finding a supplier — for him. Explain?
right: Close the tab and stay quiet

text: The CEO’s assistant says the boss wants to “see your work.” No date, no details. Prepare something?
The boss sent you a task, replied to it himself, did part of it, and asked you to “tie up loose ends.” The loose ends are the whole task. Take it?
Evening. The deputy CEO invites you to a “secret council” on whether to replace the CEO. You’re still on probation. Go?
The team lead posts “Thanks for the week, everyone!” and immediately assigns a task for Saturday. React?
The CEO announces “Innovation Week”: each department must come up with a startup. Your team is looking at you. Who’s the founder?
Your manager assigns you a task in the messenger, in email, and in the tracker — with three different deadlines. Which one?
The boss wants you to teach him “those youth words of yours” for his all-hands speech. Teach him?
HR: leadership will review salaries “in six months.” They said that six months ago. Ask for an exact date?
The department head declares “everyone should know everything about everyone” and adds a shared task sheet. Your row is visible to all and looks modest. Pad it?
The CEO decides to run the department’s work channel himself. He posts every ten minutes and demands reactions. Now what?
6:25 p.m. Manager: “Great job today, you can leave early.” It’s 6:25, and the workday ended at 6:00. Make a joke?
Evening voice message from the CEO: “Thought of you while watching a show about bees.” No explanation. Reply?
The deputy director wants a project “risk map” by 11:00. The biggest risk, in your view, is him. Include it?
New policy allows remote work “in exceptional cases, with manager approval.” Your manager is in meetings all day. Wait?
The boss holds a “feedback day”: everyone tells him what he’s doing wrong. The first two who spoke were sent to training. Your turn.
The department head mixed up your project with a coworker’s and is chewing you out for their mistakes. The coworker is sitting right there. Now what?
The CEO orders a screensaver with his portrait and motto on every computer. Your monitor now stares back at you. How do you live?
7:45 p.m. The boss asks you to watch his kid in the meeting room during an important call. The kid is already coloring on your report. Stay?
The team lead started an evening “brainstorm” in chat. No ideas, but silence isn’t an option — he tracks read receipts. What do you write?
Your manager sent a task at 8:00 and at 8:03 asked: “How’s it going?” Your progress so far: waking up. Be honest?
New rule from above: every morning, send leadership an hour-by-hour plan for the day. You don’t know what’s happening in an hour. What do you write?
The boss wants you to replace him in supplier negotiations. His instructions: “Be tough, but gently.” How do you play it?
The CEO walks into the department: “Who’s the most experienced here?” Everyone points at you. Something’s off. Own it?
The CFO sends you a spreadsheet “to check” where every cell’s formula references itself. “Simple task,” he writes. Fix it?
right: Send it back with a note

text: At 5:59 p.m. the department head calls you in “for a minute.” The minute becomes an hour about his vacation. Leave?
At the company party, the CEO says that “back in his day people worked 16 hours.” Everyone nods. Ask what his job was back then?
The team lead blocks “Deep Work Time” on your calendar — then books a call right on top of it. Which wins?
Morning email from the boss: “Who took my stapler?” CC: the CEO, the CFO, and the lawyer. Admit it was you?
The new director wants to “understand the processes” and asks you to explain your job as a public lecture. Prepare?
At lunch, your manager wants to “quickly discuss” the project right in the cafeteria. Your mouth is full. Answer?
The deputy manager wants a “part-time assistant” and offers you the job. Your current job stays full-time. Agree?
Evening message from the boss: “I feel like you’ve seemed sad lately.” You smiled all day working on his report. Reply?
Evening memo from above: “Starting Monday, everyone works in new offices.” No seating plan attached. Send a request?
The CEO arrives with a brass band — it’s the company anniversary. The band sets up at your desk. You’re mid-call with a client. What now?
The team lead asks you to onboard a newbie. The newbie turns out to be his nephew and already knows who’s “in charge.” Now what?
Friday, 6:00 p.m. The boss promises a bonus “if everything’s done by Monday.” That’s only possible over the weekend. Agree?
7:50 a.m. Front desk: “Your client is here. He decided to come early.” The meeting was set for 11:00, and your hair is still wet and your stomach empty. Go out to him?
left: Hand him a magazine, ask him to wait

text: The client dictates edits over the phone: “Make the background the color of wet asphalt after a summer rain, but not a sad one.” Write it down or ask about the shade?
6:40 a.m. The supplier's driver calls: the truck is already at the warehouse, though you agreed on 10:00. He can't wait, he's got a “schedule.” Race over there?
9:05 a.m. The bidding portal updated its form overnight. Your 40 pages from yesterday now “don't match the template.” Three hours until the deadline. What now?
Business trip. Hotel breakfast ends at 9:00, and your partner meeting is also at 9:00, across town. Eat breakfast or show up on time?
Business trip, budget twin room. A guy from the next department snored all night like a tractor going uphill. It's 6:00 a.m. Wake him or finish sleeping in the lobby?
left: Wake him and let him have it

text: Trade show morning. The rival booth next door is blasting upbeat music. Your prospect is shouting in your ear. Go deal with it?
8:15 a.m. A client sends a screenshot: your website still shows last year's prices, and he wants to buy at those. A thousand units. Agree?
New review: one star, “Couldn't get through!” The logs show the call came at 5:47 a.m. on a Sunday. Reply politely or hint at business hours?
Email at 8:30 a.m.: “I demand to speak to your manager!” Your manager is your boss, who already yelled at the coffee machine this morning. Forward it to him?
Sales is on fire. A sales guy suggests you cold-call a lead list together. The list is from 2014, and half the numbers are landlines. Start dialing?
6:30 a.m., the phone rings. A client in Khabarovsk, wide awake: “It's lunchtime here, let's go over the estimate!” You're still under the covers. Answer?
The freelance translator delivered the contract two days early. The text says “party number one does the contract thing.” Accept the work?
The client wants to meet “at our HQ.” HQ is out of town: two hours by train, then a walk across a field. Go or push for a video call?
The client has a new point of contact. She politely asks: “So what did we actually order from you?” The project is six months old. Explain from scratch?
The supplier sent fabric samples for the uniforms. All seven differ from the catalog, and one smells suspiciously like a Christmas tree. Send them back?
right: Pick the pine one, it's cute

text: A partner calls and insists you sign an NDA first, and only then will he tell you why he's calling. Sign blind?
Business trip. Your suitcase flew to another city, and negotiations are at 10:00. You're in sweatpants and airline slippers. Go like that?
The tender client asked a clarifying question. An honest answer would basically reveal your price to competitors. Answer honestly or vaguely?
The client set up a breakfast meeting, ordered half the menu, then remembered an “urgent call” and left. The check is on the table. Pay with your own card?
The client asks you to sign emails “With warmth and care” — “that's how we do it here.” Your company uses “Best regards.” Play along?
9:00 a.m. Twelve emails from one client, each clarifying the last. The final one: “Forget everything I wrote above.” Read all twelve?
The cleaning contractor asks if they can toss the “pile of old paper” in the meeting room. It's your signed tender documents. Run?
A key partner asks you, “as a friend,” to take his nephew as an intern. The nephew can't spell and dreams of an “easy job.” Help out?
The client will sign a big contract on one condition: you sing at their company party. The song is picked: three verses and a key that doesn't exist. Agree?
7:05 a.m., unknown number: “Hi, did you leave a request on our website?” The voice sounds suspiciously like the client you turned down yesterday. Answer?
The distributor sent the morning sales report. Under “Reason for decline” it says: “Mercury in retrograde.” Accept that explanation?
right: Post it in the chat for laughs

text: The customs broker wants a photo of each of the 500 boxes in the shipment by lunch, “for the records.” The warehouse is on the edge of town. Go take pictures?
The client writes: “Need the proposal by 10:00 urgently, but take your time.” It's 9:20. Is that an order or permission?
Business trip, morning. The cabbie takes you to the meeting by a “shortcut” through three villages, with a stop at his mother-in-law's. Object?
On a morning call, the client keeps calling you Vitaly. You're not Vitaly. The call's been going for twenty minutes, and it feels too late to correct her. Now what?
The trade show organizer says your booth landed next to the restrooms. But it's “high foot traffic.” Demand a new spot?
Monday morning. The client replied to the email you sent Friday at 6:58 p.m. with one word: “Well?” Is that good or bad?
The client wants “every presentation from the last five years to form an opinion of your company.” Half of them are embarrassing. Send them all?
The client's assistant says the director will see you “sometime between nine and six.” The meeting matters. Sit in the lobby all day?
9:30 a.m. The client swears he paid yesterday. No money in the bank. He sends a screenshot of the payment dated September 31. Point out the date?
The client's intern sent “edits from management.” The file metadata says the intern made them himself at 3 a.m. Make the edits?
The paper supplier emails: “Congratulations! You're our millionth customer!” The prize: a year's supply of paper clips. Pickup at your expense. Claim it?
left: Claim it for the whole team

text: 6:15 a.m., airport. Your business-trip flight is delayed four hours. Negotiations are at noon. Reschedule or run the meeting from the gate?
The client sent edits as a diagram on a napkin, photographed at an angle, with a coffee stain. Is the stain an edit or not?
left: Treat the stain as an edit

text: The client wants you to come “see on site” the warehouse you're fitting out. It's −4°F outside and the warehouse isn't heated. Go?
The sales director hands everyone a quota of “a hundred calls a day.” You're not in sales, you're in Accounting. Tell him?
left: Remind him of your job title

text: Building security won't let your client in without a pass, and you forgot to request one. The client is already calling, annoyed. How do you get out of this?
left: Meet him and walk him in

text: The client wants “everyone working on the project” at the meeting. That's eighteen people. The meeting room seats six. What do you do?
The print shop calls at 8:00 a.m.: the catalogs are ready, but the cover came out “slightly orange.” You ordered blue. Accept it?
The office coffee supplier offers a tasting right now: twelve blends, “just to try.” It's 9:15 and the report is due. Taste?
A foreign partner sent an email made entirely of emoji: handshake, rocket, money bag, and a question mark. How do you reply?
A client called you by mistake: he meant to call his mom. While you're both embarrassed, he suddenly remembers he's unhappy with the deadlines. Seize the moment?
You accidentally hit “Reply All” on a client email with “This bore again.” The bore himself is on cc. Recall it?
A partner asks you to stop by before work “for five minutes to sign a paper.” He lives an hour away in the opposite direction. Go?
Business lunch. The client is ordering his fifth course and talking about fishing. Looks like he'll discuss the contract only over dessert. Order dessert yourself?
In negotiations, the partner generously offers to “meet in the middle.” Somehow his middle is above your starting price. Point that out?
A competitor protested the tender you won and wants your certificates checked. One certificate seems to have expired a day early. Come clean?
The client came “to see how you work,” sat next to you, and comments on every mouse move: “Why did you click there?” Ask him to move?
right: Send him on an office tour

text: Product demo for a client. Two minutes in, the internet dies. The client checks his watch. Improvise or reschedule?
The supplier mixed up the address and brought you 600 pounds of nails. He asks you to “just hold them till Monday” in your meeting room. Agree?
2:00 p.m. The electrician cut power to the whole office “for five minutes.” It's been an hour. Your laptop died, and the client needs a file by 3:00. Where to work?
Lunch break at the trade show. The only food is a hot dog priced like a nice dinner. You can't leave the booth unattended. What now?
left: Blow it all on a hot dog

text: Business trip. Instead of talks, your hosts take you on a three-hour plant tour in a hard hat. They promise to sign “after Shop No. 7.” Go along?
1:10 p.m. You finally bite into a sandwich, and a client calls: “Is now a good time?” Your mouth is full, and it's an onion sandwich. Pick up?
An unhappy client came to the office in person with a twelve-page complaint. He wants to read it aloud, with feeling. Listen?
left: Hear him out to the end
right: Suggest he leave it in writing

text: The client asks for a reference letter about his own company for another vendor: “You know us better than anyone, just write it.” Write it?
2:30 p.m. The client wants back the font he rejected three rounds ago, “but a little bolder.” You deleted the old files. Recreate it?
A customer asks for a “loyal customer” discount. It's his first purchase, and he hasn't paid a cent yet. Give him the discount?
right: Offer one on his second order

text: A partner wants a photo together for social media “right now, in front of the logo.” Your shirt is wrinkled and there's coffee on your tie. Pose?
The client asks you to sign a backdated completion certificate, “because our quarter is closing.” Accounting will object. Sign?
Your conference talk is scheduled for 1:30 p.m., right after lunch. Six people in the room, two asleep. Deliver it as planned?
right: Cut it in half and leave

text: New tender requirement: a video about the company. Due today by 5:00 p.m. Budget: zero. You have a phone and coworkers. Shoot it?
On a video call, the client demands everyone turn their cameras on. His own camera is off and, judging by the sounds, he's eating soup. Turn yours on?
The promo plant sent 500 mugs for a client. The logo is printed backwards. The gifts go to the client tomorrow. What now?
A supplier's rep hints that if you pick them, there's a “nice holiday gift” in it for you personally. No holidays are coming up. Your move?
A client asks for your personal number “for emergencies.” You know him: he has an emergency every day at 11 p.m. Give it?
A foreign partner treats you to lunch from his home cuisine. The dish, he says, is “just a tiny bit spicy.” Your eyes are already watering from the smell. Eat?
Hour three of negotiations. You badly need the restroom, but the partner is about to agree on price. Step out and the moment's gone. Hold it?
The client adores your coworker and wants to work only with her. She's on vacation until month's end, and the contract is urgent. Tell him?
1:00 p.m., trade show. The brochures ran out, and the crowds are just arriving. The print shop is across town. What do you hand out?
Business trip. The hotel Wi-Fi is down, and the proposal is due at 3:00 p.m. The café across the street has coffee and an outlet. Go?
A client hired a secret shopper to test your support. He called and got you while you were arguing with the printer. Confess right away?
The client sent a “small mood board for inspiration”: 400 images, including kittens, a sunset, and an engine blueprint. Study them all?
You're in the dentist's chair with your mouth open. Your most important client calls. The dentist is holding the drill and waiting. Pick up?
right: Let it ring into the void

text: The client wants “one more little version” of the logo. It's version fifteen, and he liked the first one best. Pass off the first as new?
Tender results: you lost to a competitor by one dollar. A month of prep. Management wants you to “analyze the reasons.” How do you write the report?
A supplier offers 3% off if you write a glowing review on their website. Their deliveries are late every single time. Write it?
The client filed a complaint: there's a typo in the catalog description of his own product. He wrote that description himself. Point that out?
The partner is an hour late and texts: “Start without me.” The meeting is with him alone. Sit alone in the meeting room?
In negotiations, your coworker cheerfully tells the client: “Oh, we'll do it for half price!” You haggled two hours for full price. How do you save it?
The client states the task: “Like the competitors, only better, cheaper, and by yesterday.” Then adds: “You can handle that, right?” Your answer?
right: Offer to pick two of three

text: The catalog photographer shoots products on his phone, holding it in one hand and a gyro in the other. Says: “We'll fix it in post.” Step in?
The client added his wife to the project chat: “She's a designer, she has opinions.” She already has one, and it differs from his. Whose side?
The client invites you to the factory cafeteria: “Best meatballs in the state!” Lunch takes two hours with travel, and your report is due. Go?
Per diem is $25 a day. A business lunch near the meeting costs $50. Accounting wants receipts. How do you eat lunch?
right: Grab a pastry at a kiosk

text: You're told to call 50 clients and ask, “Rate us from zero to ten.” Client number three tells you about his divorce instead. Listen?
right: Politely get back to the rating

text: The client sends voice messages straight from the construction site: jackhammers, shouting, and only now and then the word “estimate.” That's eight so far. Decipher them?
Presentation at the client's office. Their projector won't detect your laptop; their IT guy “will be here in an hour or so.” Draw it all on the whiteboard?
You're organizing a client party. The agency's emcee needs a volunteer for a “blindfolded” game and is looking right at you. Go?
On a video call, the partner swears he's at the office working on the contract. Behind him: palm trees, the sea, and a seagull. Believe him?
A customer complaint on social media got a thousand likes. The boss wants a reply that's “witty, but no drama.” Joke or apologize?
The supplier calls: his warehouse flooded and your paper is “a little damp.” He offers to blow-dry it and sell it at half price. Agree?
The client wants a small tweak “as a favor, for free.” The developers estimate this small tweak at forty hours. Say no?
5:58 p.m. You've got your coat on. Client: “Got a minute? I'll share my screen.” Forty tabs open, and he can't remember which one he needs. Stay?
9:30 p.m. Message from a client: “Still up? Just one tiny edit, literally a comma.” You're under a blanket with a show on. Reply?
The talks went well, and the partner invites everyone to karaoke to “seal the deal.” You sing like a creaky old door. Go?
Business trip, banquet. The host announces: “The next toast is from our guests!” Everyone looks at you. Speak?
The overnight train home from the trip. In your compartment: the client's buyer you argued with about price for three hours today. All night together?
Last evening of the trade show. The next booth offers to swap leftover swag: your pens for their bottle-opener keychains. Swap?
In the evening you spot a review: “The manager with your name was rude.” You don't remember this customer at all. Reply?
7:10 p.m. The supplier sends a new price list: everything is up 25%, “effective tomorrow morning.” Rush an order at the old prices?
11:30 p.m. The bid is due at 11:59, and the bidding portal won't load. You refresh every ten seconds. Call support?
10:00 p.m. A client from the other side of the world calls: it's a bright morning there, and he wants to “go over the plan.” You're brushing your teeth. Pick up?
8:00 p.m. A contractor sends forty questions about the spec, signed: “Answer by morning or the deadline slips.” Answer tonight?
Friday, 6:30 p.m. The client signs off on the project and adds: “Just one tiny thing by Monday.” The tiny thing will eat your weekend. Agree?
A client sent you a gallon jar of honey from his own apiary. Delivery is cash on delivery, at your expense. Accept it?
Evening, grocery store. A client spots you at checkout and starts discussing the estimate while the cashier rings up your frozen dumplings. The line sighs. Talk?
6:31 p.m. Complaint from a client: “Why haven't you answered yet?!” His email came at 6:25 and just said “So how's it going?” Reply?
Business trip. Through the thin hotel wall, someone is loudly discussing a sales proposal. Sounds like competitors, pitching your client tomorrow. Listen?
left: Listen with a glass to the wall

text: Flight home from the trip. Your seatmate is the client's CEO. He wants to “talk strategy” for all three hours. No sleep for you?
6:10 p.m. The client is finally ready to sign. One condition: “Only if you come right now.” He's across town. Go?
10:15 p.m. A partner sends a photo of the receipt from yesterday's dinner together: “Split it?” You only drank water. Pay?
right: Reply with a photo of your water

text: 8:00 p.m. The client is on a call from his car. Every two minutes he drives into a tunnel and asks, “Repeat the last part.” Keep repeating?
7:45 p.m. Email: “Sending final edits!” No attachment. The client has already logged off and is on vacation till Monday. Now what?
9:00 p.m. The office renovation contractor sends a photo: the ceiling is painted pink instead of white. He wants you to confirm by morning that “it's even better.” Confirm?
11:05 p.m. A client cc's your boss: “Why is nobody answering?!” He sent his first email at 10:59. Reply tonight?
right: Reply to both in the morning

text: In the evening, a competitor's manager calls offering to “agree nicely” on who bids what in the tender. Your answer?
A client friended you and is liking your five-year-old photos tonight. Yesterday he turned down your offer. Is it a sign?
After the trade show you have two hundred business cards. Each one needs an email. In a week they won't remember you. Write tonight?
A partner invites you to the sauna “to seal our agreements.” Starts at 9:00 p.m. There are no agreements yet. Go?
In the evening, a client sends an 18-minute video message. He spends the first five minutes finding the right angle. Watch it all?
7:30 p.m. A supplier calls to wish you a happy birthday. It's not your birthday. It's your predecessor's, who quit two years ago. Correct him?
A happy client wants to record a video testimonial right now, “with you in the shot, nice and natural.” You've been on your feet ten hours and look it. Film it?
8:15 p.m. The talks dragged on, and building security is turning off the lights floor by floor. The partner doesn't notice. What do you suggest?
Web inquiry: “Big order. Call only after 10 p.m., I'm at work during the day.” It's 9:50 p.m. Call from home?
Business trip, free evening. Your hosts already bought you a ballet ticket “for the cultural program.” The ballet runs four hours. Go?
6:45 p.m. The client writes: “Please take a look over the weekend, nothing urgent.” Attached: a 120-page contract. Read it this weekend?
A customer returned an item with a note: “Didn't match my mood.” The item is a cement mixer. Refund him?
right: Ask what's up with the mood

text: The project is due tomorrow at 10:00. The contractor who did half of it hasn't picked up since 5:00 p.m., and his status says “last seen recently.” What now?
8:30 p.m. A foreign partner sends a contract in German and wants it signed by 9:00 a.m. Your German is “Guten Tag” and that's it. What now?
The client left his umbrella and jacket in the meeting room. He calls: “You're driving past me, right? Drop them off.” He lives an hour away in the other direction. Do it?
6:20 p.m. A vendor agency calls for the third time this week: “Where's our payment?” Accounting left at 6:00. Promise tomorrow or pass the buck?
You're invited to the client's company anniversary. Everyone stands and sings the company anthem. You don't know the words, and the client is looking right at you. What now?
7:20 p.m. In the shared doc you see the client's cursor deleting your best paragraph in real time. Message him or just watch?
5:40 p.m. A sales guy asks you to “play a difficult client” so he can practice for tomorrow's meeting. It'll take at least an hour. Help?
The show has closed, and hall security won't arrive until 9:00 p.m. You can't leave the booth with the samples. Wait till nine?
right: Cover it in plastic and go

text: Business trip, 10:00 p.m. The hotel lost your reservation and offers a cot in the conference room “with a great projector.” Agree?
6:50 p.m. It hits you: today is your top client's company anniversary, and you haven't congratulated them. Five hours left in the day. What now?
In the evening, a client calls from vacation: surf and screaming kids in the background. “Send me the deck, I'm bored here.” Right now?
9:00 p.m. Email: “Congratulations, you won the tender!” You open your bid: the price is missing a zero, which puts it below cost. What now?
right: Have tea, deal with it tomorrow

text: The client asks you to shout out his company on your personal socials: “A few kind words, you've got lots of followers.” You have 46, half of them relatives. Post?
8:10 a.m. A client sends a thank-you email for the project and names only you. Six people worked on it. Forward it to the team chat?
Morning train to a business trip. The deck isn't done, your laptop is at 8%, and the car's one outlet is taken by a kettle. What now?
A partner arrives at the morning meeting with a gift: a cactus as tall as a person. There's nowhere to put it, and you can't toss it: “It's from my garden.” Where does it go?
The client wants a progress report every morning by 8:30, “just to stay in the loop.” The work is still at the “waiting for your data” stage. Write them?
The furniture supplier delivered new office chairs without casters: “Casters are a separate line item.” The chairs are already at the desks. Pay extra?
8:40 a.m. A client calls: “Your guy left his laptop here yesterday.” It's your coworker's, and it's open on a page with pricing for other clients. Go get it?
The mockup was approved last night. At 9:00 a.m. an email arrives: “The director approved it, but didn't approve it. You understand.” You don't. Call?
An email from “the client's accounting”: urgently pay their invoice to new bank details. The email address is off by one letter. Smells like a scam. What now?
A trade magazine is interviewing your company at 9:30 a.m. There's no press office, so the spokesperson is you. No questions sent in advance. Agree?
Trade show morning. Where your booth should be, there's a honey booth. The organizer flips through lists: “Are you sure you're in this hall?” Setup is in an hour. What now?
Business trip. The rental place gave you a stick shift. You've driven automatic your whole life, and the meeting is in forty minutes. How do you get there?
A new client wants to meet “the whole team” on video at 8:00 a.m. At that hour, half the team is dealing with kids, dogs, and sleep. Gather everyone?
right: Introduce them one by one later

text: The client is holding a team-building event for vendors and asks everyone to fill out “What fruit are you and why.” Due by lunch. Take it seriously?
The client's buyer needs two more quotes “from competitors” for the paperwork. And hints that you could make them yourself. Do it?
Conference check-in. Your name is misspelled on your badge, and it turned into a funny word. Reprints have a forty-minute line. Wear it?
The client likes running meetings while jogging. Today at 7:00 a.m., three miles through the park, discussing the estimate on the move. Your last run was in high school. Run?
right: Offer to ride alongside on a scooter

text: The contract architect brings a model of the client's office to the morning meeting, sculpted out of Play-Doh. The client arrives in ten minutes. Show it?
right: Sketch a plan on the whiteboard

text: A trade show visitor wants to buy a display sample straight off the booth and has been haggling for twenty minutes. You need the sample till the show ends. Sell?
The client asks you to show his foreign guests around town “for three hours or so, you're a local.” You've lived here two years and know the route home–office. Agree?
Contract signing. The partner pulls out his “lucky pen” and insists everyone sign with it. The pen won't write. Everyone stares at it in silence. What now?
left: Scribble on a napkin to fix it

text: Important meeting at the client's. Your phone rings loudly with a kids' cartoon theme. The client stops talking and waits. How do you get out of this?
The tender needs a notarized copy by 3:00 p.m. The notary went to lunch “till two, or maybe three.” Wait by the door?
A client in your office decided to make himself a cappuccino and broke the coffee machine. The team stares at you in silent reproach. What do you tell the client?
right: Ask him to pay for repairs

text: A sausage supplier invites you on a factory tour with a tasting. It's an hour and a half away, but they promise “a lunch you'll never forget.” Go?
The business lunch with the client is over. You both reach for the check, and the client's hand freezes halfway. Pay for both?
At a meeting, the client changes the requirements, and they flatly contradict the signed contract. Everyone nods. Speak up now?
left: Raise your hand and say it

text: The company next door complains that your client talks in the glass meeting room are audible through the wall. Especially your laugh. Carry on?
During the meeting, the client's rep falls asleep in his chair. His colleagues pretend not to notice. Continue the presentation?
The client wants to leave you a review but asks: “Write it yourself, as me, with a couple of typos so it looks real.” Write it?
4:00 p.m. Sales asks you to upsell the client an “extended warranty” on a product that lasts forever. The client trusts you. Offer it?
Business trip. The partner's plant director asks you to address the workers in the cafeteria “about the outlook.” They're eating soup and not expecting a lecture. Speak?
left: Keep it short, add a joke

text: A partner insists his logo be bigger than yours at a joint event. Your marketer is already drafting a resignation letter. Give in?
The client sent a doc with 47 comments. Thirty of them say the same thing: “Think about this.” Think about what, unclear. How do you respond?
right: Set up a call to go through it

text: The booth builder bills you for an “extra outlet” at the price of a nice TV. Without it, the screen won't work. Pay?
Mid-call, the client brings in his lawyer: “Let's cover the legal side right now.” Your lawyer is out sick. Keep going?
The client wants a website “like that pizza place has.” The pizzeria closed last year, and the site now sells tires. Look into it?
After an evening meeting, the client offers you a ride. A huge dog lives in his car, and you're allergic. The subway is far. Accept?
6:20 p.m. Supplier: “Your order has shipped!” You open the packing slip: 1,000 boxes instead of 100. The truck is already on its way. What now?
Business trip. Your airport cab never showed, and the flight is at 9:00 p.m. The driver texts: “Stuck, there in an hour.” How do you get there?
The client invites you to the theater with his family: “It'll be fun, my wife's been wanting to meet you.” The play runs three and a half hours. Go?
Friday, 6:00 p.m. A dream tender is announced, due Monday at 9:00 a.m. Your weekend is planned down to the minute. Prepare the bid?
A client posts praise about you on social media: “Works around the clock, answers even at 2 a.m.!” The whole town sees it. Pleased?
right: Ask him to drop the 2 a.m. part

text: Over dinner, a partner offers you a job: higher pay, an office with a window. Your boss booked this dinner. Discuss it?
Over dinner, the client spills his company's inside secrets: who's feuding with whom and who's about to be fired. Stop him?
The videographer sent the client's brand video. Right in the middle: you, yawning in front of the logo. The video is already approved. Ask for a re-edit?
right: Let it go, it's kind of cute

text: The client sets a call for 7:00 p.m., “quick, fifteen minutes.” That's your workout slot, prepaid for the month. What do you do?
left: Take the call from the gym

text: In the evening, an ex-client who left for a competitor writes: “I want to come back, but with a discount for emotional damages.” Agree?
right: Take him back with a discount

text: Evening reception after the show, dress code “cocktail.” You're in a business suit, a badge, and a backpack full of samples. Go?
7:30 p.m. A client making cat food packaging sends 60 photos of his cat “for inspiration.” The sketch is due by morning, and the cat is asleep in every photo. What now?
Business trip. Your hosts are taking you on an “overnight fishing trip — that's how we sign deals here.” You're in a suit and dress shoes. Go?
11:00 p.m. You're expecting the signed contract today, and the client sends an auto-reply: “On vacation until the 20th.” Today is the 3rd. What now?
Evening tender verdict: “Bid rejected: font does not meet requirements.” The whole bid is in the right font except one footnote. Appeal?
6:00 p.m. A supplier invites you to an “exclusive product preview” with a buffet. You don't need the products, but the buffet is excellent. Go?
7:30 a.m. The client sends a photo of his fried eggs: “This is the color we need for the packaging.” Yolk or white, he didn't say. Ask?
Business trip. At 5:00 a.m. the front desk wakes you: “Your wake-up call!” You never ordered one, and the meeting is at eleven. Complain?
left: Give the clerk a piece of your mind
right: Get up and prep for the meeting

text: A supplier asks everyone at your company to vote for them as “Supplier of the Year.” They need twenty votes by lunch. Rally the team?
The client writes: “We need to meet urgently today. Any time except today.” You reread it three times. Ask what he meant?
An invitation to speak at an industry forum. Fine print: “Speaker fee: about the price of a used car.” The boss already forwarded it: “Interesting!” Your reply?
left: Explain the fee to the boss

text: The client's IT guy calls and asks you to read him your server password: “For the integration, urgent.” He sounds very sure. Read it out?
The client wants your logo removed from all his documents: “We don't like other people's logos.” It's hard-baked into the template. Redo them?
The client invited you to his morning stand-up “to fill the room.” They've been discussing their accounting for two hours. Camera off and do your own work?
The client returned the contract with handwritten edits. The handwriting is like a doctor's after a night shift. One edit could be “yes” or “no.” How do you read it?
The distributor wants you to train thirty of his salespeople. Today at 9:00, in a warehouse, no projector. You found out at 8:15. Go?
Morning coffee break at the conference. Next to you stands the director of your biggest prospect, studying the cookies. Go introduce yourself?
Business trip. The partner's office park: twelve identical gray buildings, all labeled “B.” The meeting is in ten minutes. What now?
A small-town client wants the original contracts delivered in person: “We don't trust the mail.” The next train is at 6:00 a.m. Go?
A partner sent a “preliminary” delivery schedule for the next three years. One delivery is set for February 31. Point that out?
The client sent edits entirely in capital letters. Reading them feels like being yelled at first thing in the morning. Reply in kind?
Morning, office building elevator. A stranger reads your badge: “Oh, you're with the company that blew our deadline?” Twelve more floors to go. Your answer?
left: Hear him out, get his info
right: Get off at the next floor

text: The client renames the project for the fifth time. It's now “Phoenix 2.” The contract, folders, and invoices all have different names. Rename everything?
The supplier's truck fell through, so he's hauling the whole order himself in an old sedan: trip number seven. Each time he asks for help unloading. Help?
right: Wait for him at your desk

text: Your key client calls right when you're in the restroom. It's his third try in half an hour. Pick up?
A partner who sometimes competes with you asks “as a friend” for your client's contact info. Promises he “won't poach.” Share it?
The client demands the name of the employee who made the error in the report. It was the intern, who is still crying in the kitchen. Name names?
Business trip. Your partners fed you a six-course lunch, and in an hour the next meeting — also with lunch. You couldn't fit in a cup of tea. What now?
The client asks about a product feature that doesn't exist. The sales guy already said “Of course it does!” and is looking at you. Back him up?
A school field trip reached the trade show. Thirty kids swarm your booth demanding stickers. You have none. How do you survive?
The client wants the deck “shorter, but with everything in it.” It has forty slides, and “everything” is forty slides. How do you cut it?
Negotiations. The partner sets an hourglass on the table: “You have three minutes to convince me.” The sand is already running. What now?
The tender client asks for fifty product samples “for evaluation.” Free, shipped at your expense. Send them?
The contractor offers to “optimize” the estimate by cutting the “safety measures” line. Nice savings, but the liability is yours. Agree?
right: Kick it up to the boss

text: The client will only talk in his favorite messaging app, which you've never heard of. Signup wants a passport photo and your grandmother's maiden name. Install it?
A client gave five stars but wrote: “The courier was three hours late, but thanks anyway.” Reply to the review?
The client showed up to the meeting with nine coworkers. Your meeting room seats four. No more chairs. Where do you hold it?
The client's inspection team is making a surprise visit to the site. They'll be there in an hour. The crew is at lunch, and the foreman went for gyros. What now?
6:05 p.m. The client answered your 20-page proposal with one word: “Ok.” Is that “ok, deal” or “ok, leave me alone”? Ask?
A supplier offers a “free trial,” but the contract must be signed right now, before 7:00 p.m. Twelve pages of fine print. Sign?
10:40 p.m. The print shop calls: the press broke, and the run won't be ready for the morning show. There's one printer at the office. What now?
Business trip, a free evening in a new city. You could stroll the waterfront, or run through tomorrow's presentation one more time. What'll it be?
8:30 p.m. A partner calls from a loud bar: “Let's go over the numbers real quick!” You catch every third word. Discuss?
Friday, 6:01 p.m. The client writes: “Have a great weekend!” At 6:02, another email: “By the way, one little task for Monday.” Reply?
An evening complaint from a client: “Your employee was too polite. That's suspicious.” The employee is you. How do you respond?
For your anniversary, a partner sent a cake the size of a wheel, with his logo on it. You're taking the subway home at rush hour. What about the cake?
Last night of the show. Your coworkers are off to celebrate at a restaurant, and forty boxes of samples aren't packed. Movers come at 10:00 p.m. Go with them?
11:30 p.m. The client writes: “Are you asleep?” Nothing else. You've been staring at the screen for a minute. Reply?
A partner hosts a live evening podcast and wants you as a guest in half an hour: “Talk about trends.” Everything you know about trends is from his podcast. Go on?
8:00 p.m. It turns out the wrong person signed the tender bid: he has no power of attorney. It's due tomorrow at 9:00 a.m. What now?
right: Call the lawyer in the morning

text: Business trip. Your flight home is canceled. Options: a night on an airport bench or eight hours on an overnight bus. What do you choose?
The client invites you to his birthday on Saturday: “No gifts, please!” His assistant whispers: “Everyone brings one.” Go?
7:00 p.m. A contractor offers to finish an urgent job “right now, but at double the rate.” Say no and it'll take a week. Agree?
In the evening, an unhappy client threatens to trash you in reviews everywhere unless you give him 50% off. His complaint: “the site loaded slowly.” Give in?
Dinner at a restaurant. Without asking, the client orders you “the signature fish.” You haven't eaten fish since childhood. The waiter is bringing the plate. What now?
left: Eat the fish and praise it

text: 6:30 p.m. A partner suggests a “quick drive” to see a site 120 miles away: “We'll be back by night.” You haven't had dinner yet. Go?
8:40 a.m. The team chat has 214 unread messages: a fight over whose turn it is to clean the shared coffee maker. Scrolling up, you realize it's yours. Confess?
Lena at the next desk brings homemade cheese pancakes every morning and shares them only with you. Everyone's side-eyeing. Take one in front of them all?
9:05 a.m. Intern Danny asks if he can “watch how you work.” All day. With a notebook and questions. Say yes?
Arsen is forty minutes late and whispers, “If the boss asks, I was in the archive.” The archive has been locked for two years. Cover for him?
Accounting rejects your expense report for the third time: the café receipt is “not business enough.” It's a coffee and a croissant. Fight it?
right: Let it go, eat the cost

text: In the “Office Cats” chat, a coworker posted “his” cat. You've definitely seen this photo online. Everyone's dropping hearts. Call him out?
right: Post a link to the original

text: 6:20 p.m. Collecting for Galya's big birthday: $430 raised, but the robot vacuum everyone picked costs $1,200. The organizer DMs you: “Cover the rest?”
left: Chip in and be the hero

text: Roma invites you out for “just one” after work. His last “just one” ended at 3 a.m. singing with the parking garage guard. Go?
New guy Artyom has eaten lunch alone in the conference room for three days, acting like it's on purpose. Invite him to the cafeteria?
left: Invite him to join the group
right: Leave him be: maybe an introvert

text: Sales promised a client a feature that doesn't exist and never will. The client calls you, thrilled, asking where the button is. What do you say?
Your neighbor bought a mechanical keyboard. Every keystroke sounds like a stapler firing, and he's typing a forty-page report. What now?
Someone posted a dinner photo to the work chat instead of a report, captioned “Love you, babe.” Twenty people online. How do you react?
5:40 p.m. Sveta is glowing: “If anyone asks, I'm at the doctor.” Someone from IT is waiting in the parking lot with flowers. Cover for the romance?
right: Tell her to ask for time off

text: The office manager is making the kitchen duty schedule. Your pick: Monday, with a mountain of post-weekend dishes, or Friday. Which one?
Another team's lead borrowed your developer “for five minutes.” That was two days ago, and he's still over there. Get him back?
HR asks you to be a new hire's “buddy”: answer his questions for a month and take him to lunch. In return, a thank-you in the company memo. Deal?
Nina from the next row wears lily-of-the-valley perfume, and your eyes have been watering since morning. She loves compliments on it. Say something?
A courier delivered a huge cake “To our favorite team!” with no name. Nobody knows whose celebration it is, but people are already hunting for a knife. Cut it?
By 10 a.m. the “Lunch” chat is already debating: dumpling place or salad bar. It's a tie, and yours is the deciding vote. Where to?
6:10 p.m. Pasha asks for a ride home: “It's on your way.” He lives across town; you live a few blocks away. Give him a ride?
New hire Ksyusha took your desk by mistake and already set out her cat photos and a cactus. It looks very cozy. Ask her to move?
Legal sent back the contract with forty edits. Thirty of them swap the same comma back and forth. The client's deadline is tonight. Push back?
Over lunch, Vadim mentions he saw your résumé on a job site. You haven't updated it since last year. How do you respond?
Your neighbor leaves for the day with the radio still blasting '90s hits. You've got another hour, and the chorus is stuck in your head. Turn it off?
Intern Liza brought everyone homemade cookies with a note: “Thanks for putting up with me.” They're burnt. Everyone's waiting to see who tries first.
The “Gifts” chat is debating whether to chip in for the birthday of a coworker who has never once chipped in himself. Voting is open. Your vote?
Tamara has spent thirty minutes on her summer house renovation. You now know the price of every tile in the state. Her story has barely begun.
7:00 p.m. At the ropes course team building, you're paired with the chief accountant. He's afraid of heights and clutching your sleeve. Keep going?
A former coworker who quit in a blaze of drama invites “the whole old crew” out. Your boss will definitely hear about it. Going?
9:15 a.m. Grisha shows up with a huge black eye and says right away, “Don't ask.” The whole team is dying of curiosity. Ask?
Marketing wants the “most photogenic” person on your team for an ad. Your coworkers all point at you. The shoot is today at three.
5:50 p.m. Inna is crying in the conference room: her project got canceled. You were heading home, and she saw you. Go in?
In the “Smoke Break” chat, someone posted a screenshot of your email to the boss with the typo “Dear Mr. Tigerson.” Everyone's laughing.
Procurement put up a sign in your kitchen: “Procurement only.” Your espresso machine is theirs now. Is this war?
Zhenya asks you to go to a meeting in his place: “Just sit and nod.” It's a budget meeting, and the CEO will be there.
You've been put in charge of the card for the facilities manager's big birthday. The card is blank, and it's being handed over tomorrow. Make the rounds now?
Your neighbor is trying to quit smoking and chews carrots. Loudly. Every five minutes. Your head is already pounding to the beat.
Someone suggested chipping in for a coworker's dog's vet bills. The chat goes silent; everyone's waiting for someone to go first. Start it?
5:55 p.m. New guy Timur asks if it's okay to leave right at six. Everyone else is still here. What do you say?
At 8:50 a.m., intern Matvey is already sitting in your chair, “warming it up.” It's apparently a local tradition you've never heard of. Your reaction?
HR urgently needs a copy of your diploma. It's at home in a box labeled “Misc, do not open.” Go get it now?
Larisa suggests signing up for after-work yoga together: “It's boring alone.” Yoga is at 7:30 p.m., Tuesdays and Thursdays. Join?
In the company-wide chat, someone wished you a happy birthday by mistake. Yours is six months away. Forty people have already chimed in.
Eddie posted your joint project on social media as his own. You recognized it from the cover photo. Coworkers are liking it.
Holiday party. The host announces a “Who knows their coworkers best” contest and calls you onstage. Question: “What's Elena's cat's name?”
Your row rearranged the desks into a pod. Now your back is to the aisle, and anyone walking by can see your screen.
Mitya has been failing to balance a spreadsheet for an hour, quietly groaning. You know the formula in three seconds, but then he'll ask you forever.
Ilya invites the whole team to his country house for a Saturday barbecue. It's a two-hour drive, and you had plans to lie down. Go?
Karina is handing out wedding invitations all morning. Yours says “plus one.” You don't have a plus one.
The sysadmin begs you not to tell management the server crashed because of his experiment. In exchange, he promises you a new monitor. Deal?
Dasha asks you to badge her in: “I'll be there in an hour, I swear.” The system logs who badged in whom. Risk it?
Monday morning. The team chat has forty photos of other people's weekends: cabins, mountains, babies. You're expected to at least like them. Like them all?
right: Post a photo of your couch

text: Intern Oleg asks if he can call the boss by his first name, like in startup TV shows. The boss is standing at the water cooler, hearing everything.
Every morning your neighbor meditates to rain sounds on a speaker. Everyone else has already run to the restroom three times. Ask for headphones?
6:05 p.m. Igor suggests a game of ping-pong before heading out. The loser washes the whole team's mugs tomorrow.
Anya whispers that the new sales manager “keeps looking” at you. You don't even remember him. Anya awaits your reaction.
The “Party 2026” chat is picking a theme. “Pajama Party” is in the lead. Voting closes at 8 p.m.
Intern Veronica asks for the printer password for the third time. It's on a sticky note stuck to the printer itself. Answer again?
Stas offers to swap vacations: he needs your July and gives you his November. In return, he'll help with reports until New Year's.
Working late, you accidentally walk in on Oleg and Vera kissing by the water cooler. They both see you and freeze. What do you do?
Marketing sends everyone a 60-question “company culture” survey. Question nine: describe your boss in three words.
Fyodor is pushing you to enter the company ideas contest with him. The idea: hammocks in the office. Entries close at midnight.
Rita came in with a new haircut and is asking everyone, “Well?” The haircut is bold. Very. It's your turn.
Alisa walked off with your flipchart marker again. That's the twelfth marker this quarter. Open an investigation?
left: Search her drawer in front of her
right: Buy a marker on a chain

text: Coworkers invite you to a morning bike ride to the office. Start is 7 a.m. at the park; rain is forecast by eight. Sign up?
HR announces today is “No Complaints Day.” Every complaint costs a forfeit in the jar. Your neighbor is already complaining about the day itself.
Slava asks you to send him your presentation “to look at the structure.” Last time he “looked” and presented it at the board meeting.
At 5:45 p.m., the smoking area turns into the news hub. Right now they're discussing who's getting promoted. You don't smoke. Drop by?
Valya from Accounting brings fresh gossip every morning instead of coffee. Today she whispers, “People are saying things about you.” Ask?
At the holiday party, you got seated next to the CEO. He's been talking about his fishing trips for two hours. Escape to your crew?
New guy Gleb emailed the whole team his detailed life story and a full-length photo. Reply “Welcome aboard”?
A meme about your boss just landed in the team chat. It's funny. Very. But the boss is in this chat too, and he's already typing.
Zarina feels sick but won't take a sick day: “Otherwise who'll turn in the report?” You could turn it in.
Collecting for Karina's wedding. The amount is “whatever you like,” but everyone in the spreadsheet put exactly $100. You planned on $30.
Your neighbor hung a string of lights over his desk “for the mood.” It's blinking in “disco” mode right in your eyes.
6:30 p.m. For the second hour, Lyosha has been begging you to teach him pivot tables. You've already got your coat on.
Intern Kira burst into tears because the boss called her report “fine.” She thinks it's a failure. Comfort her?
Logistics wants your signature on a document you've never seen. “Everyone else signed, you're the last one.” Sign it?
Marat confesses he's in love with a woman from Legal and asks for help with a note. He wrote: “Like clause 3.2, you're irresistible.”
right: Tell him to just ask her to coffee

text: All morning the “Parking” chat has been arguing about who took whose spot. Your car is in someone else's spot. Confess?
7:30 p.m. At the escape room team building, your team is stuck in the “riddle room.” A hint costs 500 points, and the points are shared.
