text: 6 p.m. The boss wants a bonus shortlist by morning. You’re on it — at the very bottom.
6:30 p.m. HR sends an “urgent survey”: “How stressful do you find our surveys?” Scale of 1 to 10.
HR calls at 7 p.m.: “You never picked up your employment certificate.” It’s only issued until 5 p.m.
Legal in the evening: “Labor inspectors are coming tomorrow — clear all personal items off your desks.” You have a cactus and a framed family photo.
Accounting sends the whole team’s bonus spreadsheet “by mistake.” You got less than the intern.
A coworker invites you for drinks to “celebrate finishing the annual report.” You finished it for him.
The boss after work: “Could you run tomorrow’s safety briefing for me? You just read it off the sheet.”
An email: “You have not completed the ethics course. Your certificate has been revoked.” You completed it twice.
HR invites you to an evening session on “Employee Financial Health.” Tickets are $50, deducted from your bonus.
7:30 p.m. The accountant writes: “You signed the invoice in the wrong box. Come redo it tomorrow at 8 a.m.”
HR asks you to fill out a “talent pool” form. Question 1: “Where do you see yourself in 10 years?”
The team chat is sorting out who’ll attend mandatory training on Saturday. Everyone’s suddenly “sick.” That leaves you.
Fire extinguishers are being checked on your floor tonight. Yours expired three years ago. The person responsible for it is you.
Mom asks when your vacation is. You honestly say “November.” Mom goes silent, breathing heavily into the phone.
Accounting reminds you: today’s the last day to file tax deduction paperwork through your employer. The portal is down.
left: Wait for it to come back

text: The boss goes on vacation and leaves you signing authority. On the desk: a stack of documents he “didn’t get to.”
Legal suggests “just sitting with the contract” this evening — with the whole team, until 10 p.m. Pizza will be ordered.
HR invites you to star in a company culture video. The script: “Friday, the whole office dances.”
HR notifies you of a “mismatch between your position and qualifications.” You’ve held this position for five years.
A coworker brags he got himself a bonus just by emailing the CEO. He offers you the template.
The accountant sends an evening memo: “Vacation pay is calculated by formula.” The formula takes up half a page.
6:20 p.m. The boss asks you to draft the order for your own commendation — “to speed things up.”
HR invites you to an “open dialogue evening.” Questions had to be submitted in advance — by 5 p.m. yesterday.
Training sends a summer reading list: twenty books, with a report on each.
Legal wants three printed copies of a contract for a client signing tomorrow at 7:30 a.m. The printer’s already off.
Accounting in the evening: “Due to an error your sick pay was recalculated. You need to return $300.”
HR asks you to sign “consent to evening calls about work matters.” Will they fire you if you don’t? No, but “it’ll look bad.”
A colleague from accounting is stuck late on the quarterly report and asks you to bring her dinner. She’s paying.
The boss sends a voice message after hours: “Why does your timesheet show 41 hours? We don’t pay overtime.”
HR says your engagement survey feedback is “very valuable” and they want to read it aloud at the all-hands.
Accounting reminds you: the annual travel report is due tomorrow. You took 14 trips.
Legal sends the “final version” of the contract. It’s the ninth final version today.
HR in the evening: “Your profile is missing the ‘hobbies’ field.” Without it, your bonus form can’t be approved.
9 p.m. The KPI rankings are posted in the team chat. You’re second — behind someone who’s on vacation.
3 p.m. HR brings a notice of changed terms: your desk is moving to the window. Nice, but it’s drafty. Sign?
8:50 a.m. The coffee machine dispenses only hot water and flashes “Descale.” The cleaning manual is twelve pages of fine print. Take it on?
right: Run to the café across the street

text: The coffee machine now works by badge and tracks who drinks how much. Your stats — nine cups a day — are visible to the whole floor. Ease up?
left: Switch to tea to lie low

text: Chat poll: chip in for pricier beans — $10 per person. You only drink tea, and so far just one grump has voted no. Your vote?
Rita is at the coffee machine with a pint-sized mug, ordering her fifth double espresso in a row. Six people are waiting. Say something?
A sign above the coffee machine: “Last person to get coffee cleans the drip tray.” That was you. The tray is full to the brim.
The water from the cooler tastes like plastic and warehouse this morning. Someone insists it’s always like that “after a bottle change.” Drink it?
6:20 p.m. The water cooler started its “self-cleaning” and is gurgling across the empty floor as if trying to say something. Security asks you to keep an eye on it. Stay?
Pasha labeled the cups by the cooler to “save plastic.” Your name is misspelled, and the team already calls you that. Fix it?
On your fridge shelf sits someone else’s bucket-sized pot. Your lunch is perched on its lid. Move the pot?
Someone neatly cut half your cutlet out of your container with a knife. Note beside it: “Sorry, I really wanted it.” Unsigned. Your move?
7 p.m. The office manager clears out the fridge: “Anything unlabeled goes in the trash.” Among the nameless items is your favorite sauce. Claim it?
The freezer is iced over and the door won’t close. Someone’s ancient dumplings are entombed inside. The office manager wants a volunteer with a scraper.
Sveta sets up a “fair share shelf” in the fridge: anything on it is communal. You put your salad there by mistake. Take it back?
The microwave hums, the plate spins, and the soup stays ice-cold. People in line whisper that you broke it. What now?
Gena puts herring and potatoes in the microwave “for a minute.” The floor holds its breath. You’re next. Wait, or flee to a café?
The new hire is heating oatmeal in a metal bowl. Sparks are flying. He looks at you hopefully: “Is it supposed to do that?”
The cafeteria has a new cook and a new dish: “Cream of Whatever We Had.” The line at the decent café is thirty minutes. Risk it?
The cafeteria cashier knows your usual and rings it up without asking. Today you wanted to try something new. Speak up?
The only free table is next to accounting, who are loudly discussing someone’s bonuses. Possibly yours. Sit there?
The elevator stops on every floor: someone pressed every button up to 21. You need 19. Walk or endure?
It’s just you and the CEO in the elevator. He’s silently looking at his phone. Twelve floors to go. Talk about the weather?
6:45 p.m. The elevator is stuck between floors. With you: a courier with pizza for the 8th floor. “Worst case, we eat it.” Dispatch says “about twenty minutes.”
The parking guard: “Your spot was given to the CEO’s guests today.” The nearest free one is at the mall, for $20. What do you do?
right: Park by the door “for a sec”

text: 7:10 p.m. Your car is covered in notes: “You took the Head of Procurement’s spot.” There was no sign. Remove them?
The parking gate only lifts for cars, and today you came by scooter. Duck under it in full view of security?
right: Go around to the main entrance

text: The turnstile now uses face recognition. It recognizes you only without glasses and with your mouth open. There’s a line behind you.
The turnstile slams shut on your coffee. Half the cup is in your hand, half on the floor at the guard’s feet. Now what?
The AC blows right down your neck. Your neighbor, meanwhile, is hot. Turning the vent means aiming it straight at him. Do it?
Chat war: “Open the window!” vs. “Close the window!” The window is next to you, and both sides are DMing you. Whose side are you on?
Facilities taped notices on the windows: “Do not open — disrupts climate control.” The office is stuffy and everyone’s nodding off. Rip one off?
6:30 p.m. The cleaner asks you to lift your feet and chair so she can mop under your desk. You’re mid-call with a client.
right: Ask her to come back later

text: The cleaning crew wiped your desk — sticky notes and all. Your password notes are now a soggy lump. What do you do?
The guard asks you to cover his post “for literally five minutes.” It’s been twenty. Twice now someone’s tried to hand you a package for accounting. Leave?
8 p.m. Security is sealing the floor, and you’re still in your office. The alarm arms in three minutes. Grab your stuff or call the desk?
Reception keeps mixing up your name and has been sending the next department’s visitors to you all month. Three so far today. Sort it out?
Call from reception: “A courier with flowers for you.” You weren’t expecting anything. The whole team is craning their necks. Go down?
The meeting room you booked a week ago has been taken by interns with pizza. They say they “booked it too, verbally.” Kick them out?
The projector in “Everest” is broken; in “Amazon” it works, but there are no chairs. Your meeting is in five minutes. Where to?
Important meeting in the glass meeting room. Outside, a coworker is pulling faces — he thinks you’re with friends. How do you react?
The ficus in the corner has died, and the office manager asks you specifically: “Did you water it with coffee?” A couple of times you did. Confess?
The office manager bought a person-sized monstera and put it right by your desk. The leaves poke into your monitor. Protest?
The office cat, named Ledger, has settled on your keyboard. The report isn’t saved, and the screen already reads “gggggggg.” Shoo it off?
The office cat brought a “gift” to your desk — a mouse from the basement — and awaits praise. The whole team is watching.
News in the chat: the office cat got a badge with a photo and the title “Chief Coziness Officer.” It has access to every floor; you only to yours. Offended?
9:10 a.m. A hammer drill behind the wall goes “three short, one long.” A coworker is convinced it’s Morse code and is decoding it out loud. Join in?
A workman from behind the wall asks to plug his drill into your outlet. In return he’ll fix your squeaky door. Allow it?
The office is moving in a month. The office manager hands out boxes: “Start packing now.” Your desk holds six years of archives. Sort it?
right: Leave it to the last day

text: HR shows the new office plan: an open space for two hundred, your desk next to the restroom. You can swap if someone agrees. Look for a swap?
6:30 p.m. Movers are hauling furniture for the move and try to take your chair. You’re sitting on it, finishing a report.
left: Give up the chair and leave

text: Office superstition: whoever turns on the lights first in the morning gets the new project. It’s 8:05, you’re first, it’s dim all around. Flip the switch?
The guard whispers: on the 7th floor there’s an office where nobody works, but the light’s been on since 2009. You’ve just been sent to the 7th floor. Peek inside?
Timur swears that tapping the water cooler three times makes the water colder. The whole team is tapping; the cooler is starting to wobble. Join in?
Team superstition: never wash your mug on deadline day — you’ll “wash away the luck.” Today’s the deadline, and your mug has yesterday’s tea with a film on top. Wash it?
7:30 p.m. The janitor says the closet in the “Hudson” meeting room is haunted by a fired manager. The closet creaks. You need a stapler from it. Go?
Facilities hands out light bulbs one per team, only in exchange for a burnt-out one, signed for. The light above you has flickered for a week. Go see him?
New beans in the coffee machine. It smells like burnt rubber but wakes you up like nothing else. The office has split into two camps. Your pick?
Masha brought her own coffee machine from home and labeled it “Friends only.” You didn’t make the list. What do you do?
6:10 p.m. You wanted an espresso for the road, but the coffee machine is in night mode. Only the sysadmin’s secret button combo can wake it. Call him?
The water bottles ran out, and someone filled the cooler from the tap. A note on top: “It’s temporary, don’t worry.” Drink?
Lunchtime. There’s a gossip circle by the cooler. The moment you walk up, everyone goes quiet. Fill up and leave?
right: Ask: “Who are we not talking about?”

text: Note on the fridge door: “Whoever’s eating other people’s yogurts — we know who you are.” Yesterday you ate a yogurt. Yours, you think. Or was it?
Friday evening. There’s an unlabeled cake in the fridge, clearly forgotten. It’ll go bad over the weekend. Take a slice for the road?
right: Ask in the chat whose it is

text: Every fridge shelf now has a padlock. There’s one key per team, and they want you to keep it. Accept?
A timer above the microwave and a rule: two minutes max per person. Your soup doesn’t heat up in two minutes. Go for a second round?
Someone heated fish with garlic. The smell reached your office, and a client arrives in an hour. How do you save the team’s reputation?
right: Move the meeting to a café

text: It’s “Meatless Day” in the cafeteria. A cabbage patty stares back at you defiantly. Take it, or run for a burrito?
The cook found out you wrote “too salty” in the feedback book, and now serves you personally, staring into your eyes. What do you say?
6 p.m. Everyone rushes the elevators. You squeeze in last, and it beeps: overloaded. Everyone looks at you. Step out?
Building management installed an upbeat jingle in the elevator. It’s audible on every floor and gets permanently stuck in your head. Complain?
In the elevator: you and a coworker you argued with in the chat yesterday. Fourteen floors. He’s also pretending you don’t exist. Speak first?
The parking lot now has “green spots” for electric cars. Yours runs on gas, and there are no other spots. Take a green one?
Security is inspecting every car on the way out for “removal of company property.” There are eleven cars ahead of you. Wait, or go back to the office?
The turnstile is stuck open, and the guard is making everyone swear they’re an employee. Six people ahead of you are swearing oaths. Will you?
On the way out, the turnstile wants you to rate your workday with an emoji. It won’t let you out without one, and there’s a line behind you. Which do you press?
The AC is set to 60°F “to keep everyone alert.” Coworkers are in puffer jackets; you only have a blazer. Go find out who did it?
right: Do jumping jacks at your desk

text: The AC remote is locked in a box with a combination lock. Only the manager knows the code, and he’s on vacation. It’s 82°F in the office. Crack the code?
The office window won’t close — the handle broke back in spring. Heavy rain is forecast tonight, and your desk full of papers is right below it.
left: Stuff a sweater in the gap

text: The cleaner tidied your desk: pens sorted by color, papers in a neat stack. Your creative chaos is gone. Restore it?
The cleaning crew plugged an “Ocean Breeze” air freshener into every outlet. An hour later your head is splitting. Unplug it?
The guard on the radio: “Come down, someone’s asking for you. Says it’s personal.” The person wouldn’t give a name. Go down?
Reception has started a guest book: every employee leaves a “warm wish for the day.” Reception is waiting for yours. What do you write?
6:15 p.m. Reception left you a key: “Give it to the night guard.” The guard arrives at 8 p.m. Will you wait?
The lock on the “Fishbowl” meeting room broke: the door only opens from outside. You’re locked in with a client, and colleagues aren’t answering. Now what?
right: Call reception in front of him

text: The calendar shows your meeting and the director’s booked in the same room at the same time. The director doesn’t know yet. Yield in advance?
An aloe plant appears on your desk with a note: “Take care of me.” Unsigned. A week later it’s turning yellow. What do you do?
The renovation crew left a window open, and all the plants on the sill are covered in construction dust. You’re the last to leave. Wipe the leaves?
The office cat is asleep in the printer tray. An urgent contract needs printing in ten minutes. Wake the cat?
HR is holding a vote: keep the office cat, or rehome it because the accountant is allergic. Yours is the deciding vote.
6:40 p.m. The office cat climbed into your bag and fell asleep. Pulling it out means waking it in front of every cat lover on the team.
left: Wait for it to wake up

text: The workers behind the wall play the radio so loudly that your client on the call starts singing along. The call is about the budget.
9 a.m. They’re drilling into the exact wall where your planning board hangs. The board is dancing, magnets are falling. Take it down?
The foreman from next door comes to apologize for the noise and brings pastries “for the whole team.” Three pastries, eight people. How do you split them?
First day in the new office. The boxes arrived, but there’s nothing to open them with: the box cutter is packed inside one of them.
After the move, meeting rooms are named by employee suggestion. Your “Whatever” won. Now calendars say meetings are “in Whatever.” Keep it?
The evening before the move. Twenty boxes need labeling. You have one marker, and your coworkers stepped out “for a minute” and vanished.
right: Draw a smiley on all of them

text: Your new desk is by a window facing the building next door. Five yards away is another office — and a person waving at you. Wave back?
The guard confides: there’s a “lucky” restroom on the 3rd floor — whoever visits it before a meeting gets praised. Seven minutes until your meeting.
Vera insists: whoever sits at someone else’s desk in the morning does their work all day. You’re at Vadim’s desk while your lamp is replaced. Move?
The chat is investigating which kitchen mug is “cursed.” While Igor drank from the blue one, he got three reprimands. The blue one is the only clean mug.
7:20 p.m. The guard says once a year, on this very day, a 5th-floor printer turns itself on and prints a blank page. He suggests checking. Go?
The kitchen is out of spoons. Someone took the last one and seems to keep it in their desk drawer. Your yogurt awaits. What will you eat with?
The office manager declared “Bring Your Own Mug Week” and removed the disposable cups. You forgot your mug, and you need coffee now.
Someone started the dishwasher with a single mug in it. Three-hour cycle. Your mug is dirty. Interrupt it?
Someone switched the new light-up kettle to “disco” mode: it flashes every color and plays a tune. Turn off the music?
6:20 p.m. A sticky note from the cleaner on your plate in the sink: “This is your final warning.” You never saw the first ones. Wash it?
right: Smuggle it out in your bag

text: The coffee machine now shows ads: after every cup, thirty seconds about the sales team’s new product. Still drinking?
Intern Dima has spent half an hour learning latte art and hogging the coffee machine. All he makes are “clouds,” and he shows you each one. Praise him?
The cooler is leaking. Chairs were set up around the puddle so nobody slips — now nobody can reach the water. Climb through?
A note on the cooler: “Only the designated person may change the bottle.” Judging by the signature, that’s you. You just found out.
Someone keeps putting raw, unwrapped fish in the fridge right next to your lunch. Your food already smells of the sea. Find out whose fish it is?
The fridge has a motion-sensor camera: every time you open the door, a photo goes to the group chat. Your sandwich is now a star.
Friday, 5:50 p.m. Fridge cleanout: everyone takes their stuff. You find a jar of pickles you don’t remember at all. Take it?
The new touchscreen microwave only shows hieroglyphs. You pressed something at random, and it’s been “defrosting” your soup for twenty minutes.
Note on the microwave: “Whoever exploded the egg — confess, nothing will happen to you.” You exploded it yesterday. Confess?
Cafeteria promo: “Smile at the cashier, get a free lemonade.” The cashier doesn’t smile back and hands it over like evidence. Will you smile?
Coworkers invite you to lunch in the basement cafeteria. It’s cheap, but you smell like a deep fryer all afternoon, and you have negotiations at 3.
After an update, the elevator announces floors and passengers’ names from their badges. It mispronounces yours. Very loudly.
A box marked “Do Not Open” has been riding the elevator all morning. Everyone’s afraid to touch it. Right now you’re alone. Open it?
Someone parked so close your driver’s door won’t open. Climb out through the passenger side in your business suit?
A guy from the office next door parks in your spot every evening, even though he has his own. Right now he’s still in his car. Go over?
The new turnstiles use fingerprints. You have a paper cut on that finger, and the system doesn’t recognize you. The guard is “on rounds.”
New security rule: you can only go out for lunch in pairs, “for record-keeping.” Your partner is in meetings till evening. Find a new one?
left: Find a partner in the hall

text: A repairman is fixing the AC on a stepladder right above your desk. Dust is raining onto your keyboard. Move?
Window-washing day. The man in the gondola passes you every ten minutes and waves politely. You’re on a video call. Close the blinds?
5:30 p.m. The heating came on, and the radiator under your desk is so hot your thoughts are melting. The window won’t open. Stick it out?
left: Stick it out in the heat

text: The cleaner is vacuuming the meeting room during your presentation: “I have a schedule.” The director frowns. Ask her to come back later?
The cleaning crew stuck a glossy film on your monitor. Now the screen reflects you better than it shows spreadsheets. Peel it off?
7:05 p.m. The guard is doing rounds and switching off lights in every office, including yours. You’re still there, but he didn’t notice you. Call out?
Reception mistakenly gave your visitor a “Courier” badge, and he’s spent an hour walking around the office with it. He’s your biggest client. Tell him?
New reception rule: packages are handed out only from 8:00 to 8:30 a.m. Yours arrived yesterday, and you’re running late. Run?
The “Quiet” meeting room shares a wall with the kitchen. Mid-meeting, you clearly hear someone at the coffee machine discussing you.
Someone forgot to turn on the heat in the meeting room. Everyone’s in coats, and the director jokes that “decisions get made faster this way.” Joke back?
The plant on your windowsill has grown over half the window. Coworkers suggest trimming it. It’s your pride and joy. Trim it?
The janitor swears the ficus in the lobby “cries at night.” You’re working late and really do hear strange dripping. Go check?
The office cat steals pens from desks and hides them under the couch. Your lucky contract-signing pen is gone. Crawl under the couch?
Ira made the office cat a social media account, and it’s gone viral. You’re asked to take a morning selfie with the cat for its followers every day.
The renovation crew next door accidentally cut power to the whole office. Your file didn’t save. Go have it out with them?
The renovation is done, and the foreman invites you to see the result. Behind the wall: a brand-new kitchen, better than any you’ve ever had. Take a look?
The renovation goes on into the evening. When you stay late, the workers offer tea through a gap in the wall and tell jokes. Stay and chat?
After the move, half the team is on the 6th floor, half on the 9th. The stand-up is scheduled on the 7th. Your proposal?
In the new office every door looks the same, with no signs. You walked into the CEO’s office thinking it was the kitchen. He looks up. What do you say?
HR wants a video, “My First Day in the New Office,” for the portal. You still don’t know where your desk is. Film it?
Evening after the move. Your computer isn’t plugged in: the outlet is behind a cabinet you’ve been told not to move.
Superstition: whoever goes through the revolving door first in the morning will have their head spinning all day. A coworker kindly lets you go first.
Legend says whoever sits on the blue lobby couch never gets promoted again. Only the blue couch is free, and you’re dead on your feet. Sit?
Lyonya is sure that if the cooler gurgles three times in the morning, it’ll be a lucky day. Today it gurgled twice, and he suggests going home just in case. Back him?
Team superstition: never leave without turning off your neighbor’s monitor. Your neighbor left, and their screen shows a spreadsheet labeled “Do Not Close!”
Anya insists whoever eats with the engraved kitchen spoon gets a bonus. That spoon is in your soup right now. Anya looks at you hopefully. Hand it over?
Old-timers whisper that whoever breaks “the founder’s mug” gets fired. You just dropped it. Intact, but cracked. What do you do?
The office manager is giving new hires a tour and introduces you as “a local legend who survived three office moves.” They’re taking photos with you. Smile?
right: Tell the truth about the moves

text: The coffee machine switched to voice control. It doesn’t understand your “cappuccino” and has poured you hot chocolate three times. Try again?
Ilya keeps his own milk jug by the coffee machine and hasn’t washed it in a week. It sits next to your mug and is starting to smell. Tell Ilya?
6:30 p.m. The coffee machine is broken and handing out free double espressos to anyone. Coworkers are gathering; someone’s bringing a thermos. Join in?
A courier left ten water-cooler bottles right at the team’s entrance. You can only get through sideways. Haul them to storage?
They put the water cooler right by your desk. Every five minutes someone fills up and strikes up a conversation. Work has stalled. Move the cooler?
In the fridge: a jar of homemade kefir labeled “Do not touch — it’s alive.” It’s bubbling right next to your milk. Move the milk?
Every day someone moves your lunch box to the bottom shelf and puts theirs in its place. Today you caught them. It’s your boss. Say something?
Friday, 6 p.m. The fridge holds six of your lunch containers from the week — you went to a café every day. Take them home or toss them?
An intern has organized the microwave line: she hands out numbers and calls them over the PA. You’re number 42. Wait?
right: Eat it cold at your desk

text: Someone brought a toaster to the kitchen, and every morning at 9:15 it sets off the fire alarm. The toaster is actually yours. Confess?
The camera at the cafeteria checkout mistakes you for the CFO and charges your lunch to his account. Tell the cashier?
A neighboring company in matching T-shirts is eating in the cafeteria. They’ve taken every table and are singing their corporate anthem. Sing along?
The elevator arrives with a cleaner, her cart, a bucket and trash bags inside. She waves you in. You’re going to the 22nd floor. Squeeze in?
6:10 p.m. A new hire in the elevator asks: “Have you worked here long? What’s it like?” Nine more floors. Tell the truth?
The parking lot was repainted: spaces are now eight inches narrower. You parked, but you can only get out through the trunk. Re-park?
The parking lot is closed for repairs, and staff are offered a shuttle from a lot nearby: an old minibus every half hour. Wait?
A visitor with a giant bouquet is stuck at the turnstile while the guard “looks for him on the list.” The bouquet blocks the whole way, and you’re late.
Your badge works for exit but not entry. And your phone is upstairs. The guard: “You can leave — come back in tomorrow.” What do you do?
left: Call a coworker to bring it

text: The AC whistles long and low at regular intervals. Coworkers are convinced it’s you whistling. How do you prove otherwise?
The AC is now controlled by an app. The admin is an intern from the next department, and he sets it to suit himself. Ask for access?
At exactly 2 p.m. a pigeon lands on your windowsill and taps on the glass. Coworkers call it your mentor. Feed it?
5:40 p.m. There’s an incredible sunset outside, and the whole team is at the window with phones. The boss steps out of his office. Back to your desk?
right: Snap one for the boss too

text: The cleaner begs you, just once, to get your cables off the floor and onto the desk. There are twenty, and nobody knows what goes where.
The janitor is mopping the kitchen and won’t let anyone in. Your lunch is ready and waiting in the microwave. Ask to get through?
The cleaner went on vacation and left her number: “If anything gets spilled, call me.” An hour later, juice spills on the carpet. Call her?
9:30 a.m., fire drill: everyone outside. You’re in slippers with no jacket, and it’s raining. Go out?
The guard invites you to review the camera footage: “Someone’s been taking cookies from the kitchen.” Your hand is clearly visible. What do you say?
Reception put a bell on the counter. Every courier rings it three times, and your desk is closest to it. Get rid of the bell?
6 p.m. Reception is closed, and a candidate has shown up for an interview nobody remembered to cancel. Résumé in hand, hope in his eyes. Interview him?
The booking system turns off the lights if nobody moves for five minutes. You and a client are sitting still, mulling over terms. Lights out. Now what?
The meeting room is full of leftovers from someone’s party: balloons, confetti and half a cake. Your visitors arrive in ten minutes. Clean up?
“Best Plant on the Floor” contest. Your team is entering the ficus you’ve watered for six months. The CFO is on the jury. Defend it in person?
Someone watered your succulent with leftover energy drink. It looks livelier than you do. Investigate?
The office cat is sitting on the meeting room windowsill, stopping the director from closing the blinds. He asks you to “deal with the animal.”
right: Hold the meeting with the cat

text: Friday, 6:30 p.m. Whoever leaves last takes the office cat home for the weekend. That’s you. The cat’s already in the carrier.
Workers have taken one elevator; the other says “Furniture Only.” A lone chair is riding in it. Ride along with the chair?
The renovation next door breaks for lunch: from 1 to 2 it’s quiet, and everyone tries to cram a day’s work into that hour. You’re invited to lunch. Go?
In the evening, the workers behind the wall are hammering to the beat of your favorite song. Seems deliberate. Knock back?
Clean-desk policy in the new office: everything goes in a locker at night. In the morning you’re hunting for your mug in six lockers with identical locks.
The new office has no kitchen — “in a month.” You’re invited to eat lunch on the windowsill by the elevators. Lead a fundraiser for a microwave?
Out of habit, you went to the old office, though you moved a week ago. The guard recognizes you and pours you tea. Stand-up is in half an hour. Stay?
The old office’s guard calls: “Your box of mugs is still here. Picking it up today?” The old office is across town. Go?
right: Let him keep it for now

text: Superstition: whoever eats the last cookie from the shared bowl has to close the quarterly report. One cookie left, and you’re starving. Risk it?
They say the building has a 13th floor: you get there by pressing 12 and 14 at the same time. You’re alone in the elevator. Try it?
Old-timers say your desk once belonged to someone who made VP within a month. Since then, nobody lasts there. Worried?
Office legend: whoever turns off the lights last on Friday gets reprimanded on Monday. You’re last, and the lights are still on. Switch them off?
Zhenya came in with his sweater inside out: “It’s so the project turns out in our favor.” He suggests you do the same. Will you?
The guard insists a ghost courier roams the building at night delivering packages. There really is an unlabeled box on your desk. Open it?
The office manager called in a feng shui expert. Your desk “blocks the flow” and must face the wall. Agree?
Friday, 5:30 p.m. Tradition: everyone posts what broke this week. For you: the coffee machine, the elevator and your peace of mind. Be honest?
The office manager jokes that the morning coffee line goes “by rank.” Just then, the department head steps in behind you. Let him go first?
The coffee machine now dispenses notes with your coffee, like “You’re doing great!” Yours says: “Stop drinking coffee.” Offended?
The cooler is covered in reminder stickers. One — “Call Mom” — is clearly yours, and the whole floor has read it. Take it down?
6:15 p.m. The new hire at the cooler is trying to put the bottle on for the third time and keeps missing. You’re heading home. Help?
In the fridge: a pot labeled “Communal Soup.” The team has already eaten; you’re last, and the soup is suspiciously bubbling. Have some?
Morning. The fridge was switched off overnight “to save energy.” Your yogurt and butter are swimming. Complain?
The team has a “friendship fridge”: once a week everyone brings something to share. Today’s your turn, and you brought nothing. Run to the store?
5:50 p.m. You wanted dinner at the office, but the microwave has been cleaned and taped shut: “See you tomorrow!” Peel off the tape?
There’s a three-minute hourglass by the microwave. The sand is stuck, and the person ahead of you is heating their fourth helping. Object?
The cafeteria is holding a tasting of “fall specials,” and you’ve been signed up as a taster. Today: cold pumpkin soup with kvass. Try it?
Roma introduced a ritual: silent lunches “to save energy.” The whole team chews in silence, and you’re dying to share some news. Break the silence?
Tip of the day on the elevator screen: “Don’t be afraid to ask for a raise.” Your boss is next to you, reading the same thing. Say something?
7 p.m. On the way down, the elevator freezes between floors for twenty seconds every time. Coworkers say it’s “saying goodbye.” Take the stairs?
A contractor’s van is in your spot, driver asleep. The next spot is free but belongs to someone else. What do you do?
Security reports your car is blocking the garbage truck. You’re in the director’s office presenting the budget. Step out?
New badges are wristbands. Yours is neon pink: “That’s all we had left.” Security promises it’s temporary. Wear it?
The exit turnstile now displays your overtime: today, +2:47. The guard applauds. Take a bow?
The AC drips into a wastebasket, ticking like a metronome. The team starts typing to its rhythm. Move the basket?
Your window faces a restaurant kitchen. Every morning at 10 they make pancakes, and the smell drifts right to you. Open the window?
A window-cleaning robot is stuck in the middle of your window, beeping pitifully. Call the cleaning company, or get used to it?
6 p.m. The cleaner finds three pairs of shoes under your desk and asks if you’ve opened a shop. What do you say?
The cleaning crew switched to “eco products”: the kitchen smells of vinegar and lavender at once. You came for coffee. Hold your breath and pour?
The guard tells you off: you’re eating lunch on the bench by the entrance, a “visitors’ area.” There are no other benches. Argue?
After 7 p.m., everyone leaving signs a log with a reason. You write “working.” The guard asks: “On what?” Answer?
Every morning reception wishes you a good day in a tone that suggests they know something you don’t. Today they added: “Hang in there.” Ask?
Reception announces over the PA: “Your mom is holding on line three” — and says your name. The whole floor is smiling. Pick up?
The meeting room whiteboard has had someone’s diagram on it since last year, marked “Do Not Erase!” You have nowhere to write. Erase it?
Your client meeting is in the “Siberia” room, where the window won’t close. The client came in a light jacket. What now?
While misting the plants on the windowsill, you accidentally sprayed the director walking by. He stands there, wet and silent. What do you say?
In the kitchen: a potted plant with a note, “Take me home, I’m an orange tree.” One orange hangs from a branch. Take it?
Overnight the office cat played with your stapler. Under the desk are what look like every staple in the building. Pick them up?
A vet came to examine the office cat and asks the calmest employee to hold it. Everyone points at you. Hold the cat?
The drill behind the wall always starts at exactly 9:00 — people set their watches by it. Today at 9:20 it’s silent, and the team is nervous. Go check?
The workmen ask to leave a ladder and cement bags by your door “until evening.” The passage will be one person wide. Allow it?
Evening, and the team is moving to another floor. The elevator is full of furniture, you’re carrying a box up the stairs, and halfway up it starts to tear. Call for help?
After the move, you share a desk with a coworker: you sit mornings, he sits evenings. On it: his photo, a cactus and a half-eaten apple. Clear it?
The new office has an “idea wall.” A week later it holds only “Where’s the kitchen?” and “Bring back the old office.” Add yours?
Superstition: say hi to the guard first thing, and your day will go smoothly. Today’s guard is new and doesn’t answer. Does it count?
left: Keep saying hi till he answers

text: Superstition: never argue with management on a day the coffee machine breaks. It just broke, and the boss suggests “slightly changing” your project. Argue?
The guard says a guy once left at exactly 6 p.m. and became director. Ever since, everyone tries to leave at exactly 6. It’s 5:58. Run?
Old-timers insist there’s a safe behind the painting in the lobby holding “the company’s first profit.” The painting hangs crooked. Peek behind it?
Security is testing the PA system: every ten minutes a voice repeats, “This is a test, please remain calm.” An hour later, calm is running out. Complain?
The doorman at the staff entrance asks for help with his new visitor-log tablet. It’ll take “just five little minutes.” Help him?
After his shift the doorman plays the accordion in his booth. Today he asks what song he should play you as a farewell. Stay and listen?
The kitchen now has a “Who Took What” board. Under “Who took my spoon?” there are five entries, all about you. You do have the spoons. Return them?
You open a kitchen cabinet, and a hundred tea bags tumble onto you. At that exact moment, the director walks in. Your move?
left: Pick them up in front of him

text: 6:05 p.m. An after-work chat circle is forming in the kitchen. They invite you for half an hour; at home it’s dinner and a TV show. Stay?
The elevator is broken; everyone’s walking. On the 7th floor a coworker is handing out water “for the survivors.” Five more floors to yours. Stop?
The guard secretly shows you the way to the roof: quiet, sun, a view of the city. Officially it’s off-limits. Have lunch up there?
Friday, 5:45 p.m. On Monday the office closes for pest control, and everyone works from home. The team is cheering. Take your monitor home?
6:30 a.m. The alarm goes off for the third time. The snooze button is calling your name, but there’s a 9:00 stand-up you can’t be late for. Five more minutes?
7:40 a.m. The kettle picked today to die. Without hot tea you’re barely human, and the coffee shop by the station is a ten-minute detour. Now what?
The train stops dead in the tunnel. The driver announces: “We’ll be moving shortly.” You’ve been hearing “shortly” for twelve minutes. What do you do?
The cab driver asks to swing by a gas station “for just a sec.” It’s in the opposite direction, and you have a meeting at 10:00. Agree?
Your rental scooter’s battery dies halfway across a bridge. The office is half a mile away, and the scooter weighs as much as a wardrobe. What now?
right: Ditch it and call a cab

text: Traffic is at a total standstill. Your nav app suggests leaving the car by the subway and going underground. Parking there is paid and always full.
left: Ditch the car at the subway
right: Sit it out to the bitter end

text: 7:00 a.m. The cat is sitting on your chest demanding breakfast. Your alarm isn’t until 7:45. Feed him and you’ll never fall back asleep. Don’t, and he starts with the vase.
A neighbor corners you at the elevator: “Sign our petition against the parking gate!” It’s four pages of tiny print. Sign it?
8:20 a.m. Mom sends a seven-minute video: “Look, this is how you tie a scarf properly!” You’re on the subway and your earbuds are dead.
The hot water’s been shut off without warning. It’s November, and at 9:30 you’re presenting to a client. Ice-cold shower?
Your bus pulls up, but it’s so packed the doors take three tries to close. The next one is in twenty minutes. Squeeze in?
You’ve decided to bike to work. Nine miles, and the office has no shower. Your coworkers sit right next to you all day.
right: Change your mind and take the train

text: Your shoelace snaps right at the door. No spares, and the shoe slips off with every step. You need to leave in two minutes.
7:15 a.m. The dog has brought his leash and is looking at you like his life depends on this walk. It’s pouring, and you’re already in your work shirt.
Your smartwatch reports: “You slept 4 hours 12 minutes. We recommend taking it easy today.” You have five back-to-back meetings.
The commuter train is running half an hour late. The platform has a snack kiosk selling meat pies and one free bench.
left: Eat a meat pie on the bench

text: Your shirt is so wrinkled it looks slept in. The iron needs three minutes to heat up, and you don’t have three minutes.
A stranger on the subway reads your screen over your shoulder and comments: “I wouldn’t answer that client like that.” You’re typing a work email.
8:00 a.m. The fridge contains mustard, a lemon, and one egg of questionable age. Breakfast?
The alarm went off, but the pillow is extra soft today. Your brain suggests working from home, since “no one will notice.”
Your sister calls at 7:50: “Can you pick up your nephew from daycare at six? I won’t make it.” You have a call at 5:30.
The streetcar has stopped: someone parked on the tracks. The driver gets out to hunt for the owner. Passengers sigh.
Your building’s elevator is broken. You live on the fourteenth floor, and you’re carrying a laptop, a gym bag, and a bag of trash.
There’s a free car-share car right next to you, but inside it smells like a fish lived there for a week. No other cars nearby.
The barista recognizes you: “The usual? Maybe a double today? You’ve got a rough-week face.” A double costs 50% more.
1:10 p.m. The courier with your order is outside your building, calling: “I can’t wait until tonight.” You’re an hour away at the office.
left: Ask a neighbor to grab it

text: Your package is on its last day at the pickup point. It closes at 8:00 p.m., and your lunch break starts in half an hour. Make a dash?
2:00 p.m. The clinic calls: “We have an opening today at 3:30. The next one is in a month.” Your tooth has been aching for a week.
left: Ask to leave for the dentist
right: Tough it out till next time

text: The vet calls at lunch: the cat needs a booster shot, and the only slot is tomorrow at 11:00. Your quarterly report is due that morning.
The building management writes: “Tomorrow, 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., we need access to your apartment to check the meters.” You’ll be out all day.
Your childhood friend is in town for one day only and invites you to lunch at 1:00. You haven’t seen each other in five years, but your lunch is scheduled for 2:00.
Your shopping app pings: “Flash sale! Two hours only!” You’re on a boring call, and your finger is already drifting toward the cart.
The pool next to the office has an hour of open swim at lunch. Your cap and towel have been in your backpack for three months. Today?
You’re working from a coworking space. The person at the next desk is on a loud call — for some reason on speakerphone. You’re on a call too.
left: Ask them to keep it down

text: You’re working remotely from a café. The waiter asks for the third time if you’d like anything else. Your cup has been empty for ages.
Working from home. The cat is lying squarely on your touchpad, purring. Every time you move him, he’s back in ten seconds.
Your home internet dies five minutes before a client call. You could tether from your phone, but your data is nearly used up.
right: Run to the café on the corner

text: You’re working from home, and at 1:00 p.m. — official quiet hours — the upstairs neighbor fires up a hammer drill. Your call starts in ten minutes.
right: Take the call from the bathroom

text: Your personal trainer texts at lunch: “You’ve missed three sessions. Your membership expires Friday.” Your deadline is Thursday.
Dad calls at 3:00 p.m.: “My computer said something and switched off. Come over right now.” You can hear the TV running in the background.
Your brother texts: “Lend me some money till payday, I really need it.” Judging by last time, his payday comes about twice a year.
Your nephew’s teacher calls you because your sister isn’t picking up: “He ate some modeling clay. Don’t worry, but please come.”
After lunch, your back reminds you it exists. You’re sitting like a question mark. You could stretch right at your desk in front of everyone.
You’re working from home and ordered pizza for lunch. The courier calls right in the middle of a call where you’re presenting.
Friends in the group chat: “Trivia night at the bar tonight, we can’t field a team without you!” Tomorrow at 9:00 you’re defending your project.
7:00 p.m. Your partner texts: “Where are you? We had dinner plans.” You honestly forgot and you’re still at the office.
Evening. Your gym bag has been with you all day, and so has your guilty conscience. The gym’s on the way, but your legs are begging for the couch.
The corner store closes in five minutes. There’s no bread, no milk, and apparently nothing at all at home.
10:00 p.m. The washing machine beeps: the cycle’s done. If you don’t hang it up, it’ll smell like a swamp by morning. And you’re already in bed.
The building group chat demands: “Emergency residents’ meeting at 8:00 p.m. in the courtyard. We’re deciding the fate of the flower bed.” You just got home.
11:30 p.m. The episode ended on a cliffhanger. The streaming service helpfully starts the next one in five seconds.
Your guitar has been gathering dust in the corner for three years. The evening’s free, and your fingers almost remember three chords. So do the neighbors.
right: Dust it off and go to bed

text: Your neighbor with the dog steps out of the elevator just as you do: “Oh, could you look at my faucet? It’s dripping! Just a minute!” Her minutes usually last an hour.
right: Claim you’ve got a train to catch

text: Your new alarm only turns off if you solve three math problems. At 6:45 a.m., your brain can’t add seven and eight.
Your spot outside your building is taken by someone else’s car. No note, no phone number, and your car is blocked in.
Downpour. Your umbrella broke yesterday, and the subway is a ten-minute sprint away. You could wait it out in the lobby and risk being late.
right: Wait it out in the lobby

text: 8:05 a.m. Water is dripping from your bathroom ceiling. The upstairs neighbor isn’t answering, and you need to leave in ten minutes.
right: Put a bucket under it and go

text: You set your alarm for 6:00 to start running in the mornings. Outside it’s dark, cold, and raining. Your sneakers are by the door.
You’re at the door, and your keys are gone. You last saw them in a jacket pocket, and someone in the family wore that jacket. Search?
right: Leave the door to a neighbor

text: Your parrot has learned the sound of your alarm and plays it at 5:30 a.m. Every morning. With joy.
right: Cover the cage with a blanket

text: On the way to work you realize your throat is scratchy. There’s a pharmacy nearby, but there are five retirees in line with prescriptions.
6:10 a.m. Under your window, a garbage truck is clanging like it’s unloading pianos. Your alarm’s still an hour away.
left: Try to get back to sleep
right: Get up and do some exercises

text: Grandma calls at 7:30 to tell you her dream: you’re going to get an important letter. A minute later, an email from the boss arrives: “We need to talk.”
left: Hear the rest of the dream

text: Right at the subway entrance, your heel snaps. There’s a shoe repair stand on the corner, but it opens at 9:00 — and you need to be at the office by 9:00.
Tourists with a map are strolling slowly down the bike lane in front of you. Your bell is broken, and you’re running late.
On the train, a woman recognizes you: you went to school together. She wants to discuss every single classmate during the forty-minute ride.
First snow. Your winter boots are on the top shelf of the closet, and your summer sneakers are soaked through after five steps.
The hamster escaped from his cage overnight. In the morning you hear rustling somewhere behind the couch. You leave in twenty minutes.
The app reminds you: “Day 15 of 30 — morning yoga.” You only did the first three days, but the perky instructor on the splash screen refuses to give up.
Your budget cab has arrived: loud music inside, and the driver is singing along. It’s a forty-minute ride, and you need to prep for a meeting.
You wake up on your own a minute before the alarm. Fresh, rested. The clock says 5:59 a.m. — Saturday. You were sure it was Friday.
The dishwasher is beeping and flashing a mysterious error code. Your only clean mug is inside. You leave in ten minutes.
You fell asleep on the subway and missed your stop by three stations. The train back arrives in thirty seconds on the same platform.
At 7:45 a.m., your son announces he needs a carrot costume for school today. This is the first you’ve heard of it. Right now.
right: Orange T-shirt and a green tuft

text: Your daughter wants her hair “like in the cartoon, with a crown of braids.” You can only do a ponytail, and you leave in ten minutes.
The farmer from the market texts: “Your potatoes are ready. Pick them up by 4:00 today, then I’m leaving.” The market is across town.
The clinic calls at 12:30: “Your test results are in. Please come see the doctor — we can’t discuss it over the phone.” The voice is suspiciously calm.
The class parents’ chat: 147 new messages. The last one: “Who hasn’t chipped in for the teacher’s gift?” You’re in a meeting.
The daycare teacher writes at 2:00 p.m.: “Tomorrow is pajama party day. Please bring pajamas, a stuffed toy, and a pie for the whole group.”
right: Buy a pie on the way

text: Your contractor calls at lunch: “This wall’s crooked. Should I level it, or leave it since it’s getting wallpaper anyway?”
A friend texts at 1:00 p.m.: “You’re still helping me move this weekend like we agreed, right?” You don’t remember agreeing, but the chat history says otherwise.
right: Offer to buy the movers pizza

text: The bank calls at 3:00 p.m.: “Please confirm an unusual purchase: 44 pounds of parrot food.” You don’t have a parrot.
Working from home. Behind the wall, the neighbor is singing karaoke. Apparently it’s their day off.
A coworker is dragging you to yoga over lunch: “Forty minutes and you’ll feel brand new!” Which means eating lunch at your computer.
Your home camera shows the aquarium filter has switched off. The fish are fine for now, but the aquarium forum says it’s “urgent.”
You’re working from home, and at 3:00 your kid wants to go to the playground. You have a client call at 3:30.
left: Take the call from the swings

text: Your pen-pal chess opponent made a move and demands a reply: “Your move! I’ve been waiting a week.” You’ve got a task on fire.
A courier calls: “I left the package by your door like you asked.” You asked no such thing, and no one’s home. The neighbors are known box enthusiasts.
left: Ask a neighbor to grab it

text: Working from home. Your laptop wants to restart for updates, “approximately 47 minutes.” Your call is in fifteen.
Mom: “You never call anymore.” You called yesterday. Mom is already setting out teacups for a video chat.
9:00 p.m. No energy to cook. You could boil some frozen dumplings, or order food that’ll arrive in an hour.
Class reunion Friday at 7:00 p.m. Everyone will remember what you dreamed of becoming. You dreamed of becoming an astronaut.
The 7:30 book club is discussing a 900-page novel. You’ve read the blurb and half of chapter one.
The seedlings on the windowsill are wilting. Mom said to water them every evening; you watered every third. Mom arrives Saturday.
The dance studio near your home is opening an evening class: “Salsa for beginners, Tuesdays and Thursdays at 8:00.” First class is free.
10:40 p.m. Upstairs they’re stomping like they’re rehearsing a dance with stools. You have an early start tomorrow.
right: Earplugs and a pillow on your head

text: 8:00 p.m. The dog chewed up your work badge. Without it, you won’t get into the office tomorrow, and a new one can only be ordered through HR.
7:20 p.m. You’re in a cab that’s been stuck in traffic for half an hour. The meter is ticking, and home is two blocks away.
Evening. Your running app reminds you: “You promised yourself 5K!” Outside it’s sleet.
A photographer friend invites you to his exhibition at 8:00 p.m. Free entry, free wine — but you still have a report to finish.
Your gift certificate for a pottery class expires today. The class is at 7:30 p.m. You’re still at work.
Friday night. Your partner wants to see a movie, your friends want the bar, and your body wants to be horizontal. Your call.
Saturday, 9:10 a.m. Your phone buzzes: the boss has dropped a “quick question” in the work chat. You’re in pajamas with a pancake in your mouth.
Sunday, 10:00 a.m. For the first time in a month you woke up without an alarm, and the laptop on the desk is giving you a reproachful look: emails won’t sort themselves.
right: Throw a blanket over the laptop

text: Saturday, 7:00 a.m. Your parents are expecting you at their country place: fence, garden beds, barbecue. A coworker asks you to “take a quick look” at a presentation over the weekend.
Saturday, 8:00 a.m. The app with the owl warns: “Your two-day Spanish streak is in danger!” You’re under the covers.
Saturday morning. An unknown number is calling. Maybe it’s spam, or maybe it’s a client you once gave your personal number to.
8:00 a.m. Behind the wall, the neighbor’s kid has sat down at a drum kit for the first time. Huge enthusiasm, zero rhythm.
right: Escape to a café to work

text: You’ve got a podcast on: “How to Get Everything Done.” It’s been going for forty minutes, and you got so absorbed you missed your stop. What now?
A coworker from the next building messages: “I’ll drive you to the office if you’re out in three minutes.” You haven’t brushed your teeth yet.
On your jog you run into your boss, who also runs. He’s faster and clearly wants to talk about deliverables.
Your coffee maker broke, but the neighbor across the landing brews coffee so well the smell comes through the vents. Ring his doorbell?
The office elevator is broken, and you’re on the eleventh floor. The accountant is already resting at the first landing.
right: Wait for the technician in the lobby

text: Monday, 6:30 a.m. You stare at the ceiling and recall that there was a weekend, just not for you. Get up?
You’re working from home, and at 8:55 the boss unexpectedly turns on cameras for the stand-up. You’ve got a shirt on top and dinosaur pajamas below.
8:00 a.m. Mom sends a list: “Pick these up on your way: dill, ground beef, batteries, and a lightbulb.” On your way to work. Downtown.
At 6:00 a.m., your neighbor gets home from the night shift and blasts the news. Your alarm is set for 7:00.
right: Yell at him through the wall

text: At 8:10, your elderly neighbor asks for help printing a ticket for her granddaughter. She has a printer. She doesn’t have drivers.
Your jacket zipper is stuck. It won’t zip up or down, and it’s 23°F outside.
Working from a café. There’s only one outlet, and a student with three gadgets has claimed it. You’re at 5% battery.
Your new coworking neighbors are loudly celebrating their startup launch. There’s cake, and they’re inviting you too.
The contractor sends a photo: “They delivered the wrong tiles. Do we lay the green ones or wait a week?” The tiles are neon lime.
A friend is dragging you to a CrossFit trial session at lunch. He says “half an hour and you’re a new person.”
Working from home. Lunch: yesterday’s pasta from the fridge, or the cafeteria across the street. That’s ten minutes less work.
Your kid is sick, and you’re working from home all day. He wants a story, and you’ve got a call with a client.
An hour before your call, the handyman neighbor knocks: “I’m replacing outlets on the whole riser, power’s off for forty minutes.” You’re working from home.
left: Wait it out at a café

text: The dog trainer writes: “Your dog did great today, but tomorrow the owner needs to attend at 2:00.” You have a team meeting at 2:00.
Working from home. The washing machine is on spin cycle, hopping around the bathroom like a dancing elephant. It’s audible on the call.
Your grocery delivery arrived at 1:00, but instead of chicken they brought a layer cake. The courier’s long gone.
The friends’ chat “Beach trip!” hit 300 messages in an hour. They’re picking dates, and you don’t even know if you’ll get time off.
The tire shop writes: “The only slot for a tire change is today at 3:00, then there’s a two-week wait.” Snow is forecast for Friday.
Your swim coach reminds you: “Amateur meet on Saturday — you’re signed up for the 50-meter freestyle.” You swim breaststroke.
The shopping site says holiday delivery is only guaranteed for orders placed by 3:00 p.m. Your family gift list hasn’t been started.
Your aunt calls at lunch: “You’re coming to my birthday on Saturday, right? I baked a cake shaped like a 60.” Saying no is not an option.
Friends are planning an overnight camping trip this weekend. Tent, campfire, mosquitoes. No way to use a laptop. Going?
You ordered dinner, but the courier has been on his way for an hour and a half. The app shows him driving in circles around your building.
Friday, 8:00 p.m. Your friends are at the bar, your partner’s on the couch, and your laptop’s in your backpack. All three are waiting for you.
At 7:00 p.m. the gym is so packed there’s a line for the barbell. The security guard jokes about “rush hour.” Wait?
The hairdresser can only see you today at 7:00 p.m.; the next slot is in three weeks. You’re still at work and the task is almost done.
8:30 p.m. Your cousin calls: “Hey, you know people in IT, right? My computer’s frozen.” The people in IT are you.
Evening. The cat knocked your work mug off the desk and it shattered. He’s looking at you without a shred of remorse.
Your neighbors at the country house invite you to a barbecue on Saturday, but tonight your boss hinted at a “Saturday brainstorm.”
8:00 p.m. Your daughter wants to play you a scale on the violin. For the third time tonight. The scale still sounds like a creaky door.
There’s a sale at the mall tonight. A winter jacket at 50% off, but getting there means two hours in a crowd.
The remote workday drags on until 9:00 p.m., because the line between work and home has vanished. Your laptop is still on the kitchen table.
Mom showed up for a visit unannounced. The fridge is empty, and your laptop and papers are all over the couch.
Your downstairs neighbors complain in the building chat that you “stomp around like an elephant every evening.” You’re just walking around your apartment.
The pool has free lanes this evening. But your swim cap is at home, and the front desk sells a pink one with ducklings.
Your childhood friend invites you bowling at 9:00 p.m. Tomorrow’s Monday, and your personal best is one strike in 2009.
The dog ate a sock. The vet says: “It’ll most likely pass on its own, but keep an eye on him.” You’ll have to watch him all night.
11:00 p.m. The fridge is humming seductively. You promised yourself no eating after six, but there’s a slice of yesterday’s cake in there.
The scooter won’t let you end your ride: “You’re outside the parking zone.” The zone is across the street, and you’re already at the office door. The meter’s running.
right: Keep paying till it sorts itself out

text: The subway turnstile rejects your card and flashes red. A line is building behind you, along with someone’s heavy breathing.
The cab driver cheerfully offers: “I know a shortcut through the back streets, we’ll save ten minutes!” Last time, that got you stuck at a gate.
8:05 a.m. The oatmeal burned, and the smell is already in your jacket. Make a new batch, or leave with no breakfast but plenty of aroma?
Halfway to school, your kid remembers the indoor shoes. They won’t let him in without them, and home is ten minutes back.
Your alarm didn’t go off because of an overnight phone update. You open your eyes at 8:40, and your meeting is at 9:30.
Everything iced over during the night. The sidewalk is a skating rink, and the bus stop is 300 yards downhill.
7:20 a.m. Your neighbor is panicking: “Please walk my dog! I’m sick.” The dog is a huge and extremely energetic Saint Bernard.
Ticket inspectors board the train. You don’t have a ticket: the app froze at checkout. All you have is a large bill.
7:05 a.m. The courier has brought your wardrobe three hours before the delivery window. He won’t wait: “Now or next Tuesday.”
8:15 a.m. Mom: “Install that doctor appointment app for me right now, I don’t understand any of it!” You’re on the bus.
left: Set it up over the phone

text: A 7:00 a.m. swim is the best start to the day, say people who get up at 5:30. You bought a membership yesterday.
You came to a café to work this morning. The barista puts on upbeat jazz at full volume, and there are no other customers yet.
You’re leaving home, and your backpack feels suspiciously heavy. Inside, curled up on your laptop, the cat is asleep.
Your phone is at 3%, and the charger is still plugged in by the bed. Without your phone: no ticket, no map, no music.
The bus driver skips your stop: “I’m not opening the doors, next stop’s half a mile on.” The whole bus sighs.
The janitor has been mopping the stairwell since 8:00. Water is ankle-deep, and he’s glaring at your shoes. You need to leave now.
Your boxing coach texts at 6:30 a.m.: “See you in forty minutes, sparring today!” You never asked for this.
Mom at 12:30: “I’m near your office, let’s have lunch!” Mom nearby means a full menu and a full interrogation.
Your son texts at 1:00 p.m.: “I have to bring money for the field trip today or I can’t go!” Cash only, handed directly to the teacher.
A neighbor texts: “Your car’s been screaming in the yard for an hour.” The key fob is in your pocket, and the car is six miles away.
You’re working from home, so your relatives have decided that means they can visit. Your aunt is already buzzing the intercom.
At this café for remote workers, the Wi-Fi password changes every hour. The new one is posted at the register, and the line is ten minutes long.
Dad’s birthday is tomorrow and you have no gift. Courier delivery only works if you order by 2:00 p.m.
The front desk: “A spot opened up for your checkup today at 3:00; otherwise it’s a month out.” Your meeting runs till 4:00.
Your tennis buddy texts: “The court’s free at 1:00, play for an hour?” The court is across the street from the office. Lunch will vanish, though.
Bidding on a rare vinyl record ends at 2:00 p.m., right in the middle of a client meeting. You’ve been hunting for it for two years.
The dog sitter cancels the lunchtime walk: “I’m sick.” The dog’s been home since 8 a.m., and you’re at the office until six.
Working from home. The parrot has learned the word “deadline” and screams it whenever you unmute on a call.
right: Hide in the bathroom with your laptop

text: The washing machine repairman will come “between 12 and 6.” You’re working from home and can’t step away for a minute.
The auto shop calls: “Your car’s ready. Pick it up by 5:00 or it goes to paid parking.” The shop is half an hour from the office.
3:00 p.m. Your eyes are closing. Your car is in the parking lot, and it has a nice reclining seat.
Your eyes are red from the screen. The doctor says to look into the distance for twenty seconds every twenty minutes. In the distance is a coworker who will get the wrong idea.
At lunch you realize you left your pills at home — the ones you have to take at exactly 2:00 p.m. Home is forty minutes away.
Your sister is getting married and messages at lunch: “Vote now: raspberry cake or cherry?” The chat also has fifty napkin options.
Your friend is getting married and wants you to give a speech. The wedding’s Saturday, the speech is due Friday, and you’re swamped.
Your neighbor writes: “Can you take my package? It’ll come between 12 and 6.” You’re working from home, but you have five calls.
The airline emails: “May sale ends at 4:00 p.m.” Your vacation hasn’t been approved yet, but the prices are ridiculous.
left: Buy now, figure it out later

text: Working from home. Your roommate decides to vacuum right in the middle of your presentation. The vacuum is ancient and loud.
The courier made a mistake and delivered someone else’s order: blue cheese, olives, and a bottle of pricey juice. He’s already gone.
Registration for the city half-marathon opens at noon, and slots vanish in minutes. At noon, the boss walks up to your desk.
left: Register in front of the boss

text: Friends invite you to board game night and want an answer by 3:00. Game night usually runs until 3 a.m.
The cat walked across your keyboard and sent the boss “ppppppppp;;;;” in chat. The boss instantly replied: “?”
The pickup point by the office has a twenty-person line at lunch. Your order is a charger you won’t survive the day without.
3:00 p.m. Your fitness band reports: “You’ve taken 812 steps today. Time to move!” It buzzes every five minutes.
left: Walk a lap of the floor

text: Your balcony tomatoes: the soil sensor reports “Soil dry, critical.” You’re at the office until evening.
Family chat: “Who’s driving Grandma to the country house on Saturday?” Everyone is silent, waiting for someone to cave.
Friday, 3:00 p.m. The boss casually asks: “Any plans for the weekend?” You can hear the trap in his voice.
A coworker asks to swap: you take his Saturday on-call, and he’ll cover for you “sometime later.” Your Saturday is free.
Working from home. The neighbors started renovating, and it’s so loud it comes through on calls. Your manager asks whether you’re on a construction site.
The gym by the office is nearly empty during the day. You could go for forty minutes, but then you’d have to stay until seven.
Grandma calls at 2:00 p.m.: “I’ve learned video calls!” The camera shows her ear, and you’re at work in an open-plan office.
Friends are booking a lakeside cabin for the weekend and need an answer by 4:00. This morning the boss mentioned a “possible Saturday task.”
right: Wait for clarity from the boss

text: 7:10 p.m. The subway car is packed, and the guy to your right is eating a shawarma an inch from your coat.
6:30 p.m. It starts to rain, and you’re on a rental scooter. Home is two miles away; the subway is half a mile.
right: Drop the scooter at the subway

text: Friday, 9:00 p.m. Surge pricing has cabs at triple the usual fare. The bus is still running, but with two transfers.
You’re at a café with friends, and the last bus leaves at 11:10. Your friends are ordering more dessert and begging you to stay.
A coworker offers you a ride home. It’s forty minutes with him, and he’ll spend all forty discussing the quarterly report.
Wednesday, 7:00 p.m. Your parents are expecting you for dinner: Mom made “a little something,” meaning enough for twelve.
9:00 p.m. Your kid needs help with a fourth-grade math problem. You’re rereading it for the fifth time.
left: Solve it together, no matter what

text: 8:30 p.m. Your kid remembers they need a pinecone craft for tomorrow. No pinecones at home, stores are closing, the park is dark.
left: Head to the park with a flashlight

text: Evening. Your partner wants to talk about vacation plans, but yesterday’s report is still spinning in your head.
6:45 p.m. Your calendar reminds you: today is your anniversary. The flower shop closes at 7:00, and you’re still at the office.
A friend going through a breakup texts: “Can you come over right now? I really need to talk.” You just got into bed.
Your friend’s birthday is at a karaoke bar until midnight. You can’t sing, but your friend has already signed you up for a duet.
8:00 p.m. Mom calls and sternly asks: “What have you eaten today? Be honest.” Honestly: three coffees and a cookie.
Dad calls in the evening: “Coming Saturday to fix the faucet? I already bought washers and took apart half the sink.”
Evening. Stuffy nose, scratchy throat. You could take a sick day tomorrow, or pop a pill and go to work a hero.
The clinic emails in the evening: “Discount on a full checkup, Saturdays at 8:00 a.m.” You’ve been promising yourself a checkup for three years.
Thursday, 8:00 p.m. Your friends are playing pickup soccer and are exactly one player short. You. Your legs are jelly after work.
Today’s your first sparring session at boxing. The coach says “we’ll keep it light” and glances at an opponent twice your size.
11:40 p.m. You’re lying in bed mentally rewriting yesterday’s email to a client. Sleep won’t come, and your phone is right there.
left: Get up and write the email

text: You decided to go to bed at 10:00, like every article says. It’s 9:58, and there’s a fascinating video about bridge building on your screen.
You’re knitting a scarf for your brother’s birthday. The birthday is the day after tomorrow, and the scarf currently resembles a pot holder.
A 2,000-piece puzzle covers the whole kitchen table. You’re working from home tomorrow, and there’s nowhere else to work.
A friend invites you fishing on Saturday: departure at 4:00 a.m. Apparently the fish only bite at that hour, and only for him.
The self-checkout demands for the third time that you “remove the unknown item” from the scale. The item is your glove.
Online store: robot vacuum 40% off until midnight. You hate vacuuming, but you also hate spending money.
10:30 p.m. The courier calls: “I’m at your entrance.” He’s at the building next door. And has no plans to come to yours.
Your neighbor brings a pie: “Help yourself!” Then she settles into your kitchen to tell you about every resident in the building.
The neighbors next door are throwing a housewarming. The music’s loud, but they knock on your door: “Come on in! We’ve got barbecue!”
Your neighbor is going on vacation for a month and asks you to water his plants. There are twenty-eight of them, each with its own schedule.
The cat hasn’t eaten all evening and looks sad. The 24-hour vet is across town.
8:00 p.m. The dog is standing at the door with his leash, and you’re on a call with colleagues in another time zone. It’s morning there and they’re bursting with energy.
left: Take the call on the walk

text: 9:00 p.m. A call with colleagues from the other side of the world. For them it’s noon and full of enthusiasm; you’re already in pajamas.
Sunday, 9:00 p.m. The Monday dread is creeping in. You could sort your email now so the morning is easier.
Your family is going to a fair on Saturday: honey, cheese, pony rides. And you’ve got an unfinished presentation for Monday.
Friends are heading out of town for the weekend. Departure Friday at 7:00 p.m., and you have the weekly wrap-up meeting at 6:30.
The hallway lightbulb burned out. No stepladder, just a three-legged stool.
9:30 p.m. Pack lunch for tomorrow, or eat in the cafeteria with your coworkers again?
Sunday, 8:00 p.m. Five shirts for the week need ironing. The iron is waiting for you. You’re waiting for it all to happen by itself.
The robot vacuum is stuck under the couch, beeping pitifully. The only way to free it is to move the couch.
Online English lesson at 8:00 p.m. You haven’t done the homework, and the teacher always starts with it.
Parent-teacher meeting at 6:30. They’re discussing curtains for the classroom. Only your vote on the color is missing.
It’s Grandma’s birthday. Calling means talking for at least an hour. Not calling means hearing about it from Mom for a week.
The neighbor’s cat is sitting on your balcony demanding dinner. The owners are away for a week, and the cat clearly knows it.
You’re working from a café, and at 9:00 p.m. the waiter starts flipping chairs onto tables. The report is almost done.
You’re almost home when you realize your keys are on your desk at the office. Office security is there until 9:00 p.m.
Your own scooter died at the office. The charger’s at home, and the only outlet in the office is taken by the kettle.
8:40 a.m. Your inner voice suggests starting the day with the scariest task. Your other inner voice suggests tidying your desk first. Which one do you listen to?
You’ve opened the same report three times and closed it three times without starting. Your inner voice suggests “making some tea first.”
A pigeon has moved into the Olympus meeting room. It sits on the projector, looking at you like you’re the guest. Your meeting starts in ten minutes.
left: Shoo it out with a folder
right: Hold the meeting with the pigeon

text: A 40-tab master spreadsheet has broken: every cell now says “#REF!” The last person to save it was you.
left: Fix it by hand till evening

text: You bought the course “Become Productive in 21 Days” and haven’t opened a single lesson. Today is day 19. Catch up tonight?
A new poster by the water cooler: “Fatigue is weakness leaving the body.” Someone has already added in marker: “Along with my will to live.”
left: Snap a photo for the chat

text: Surprise audit: an inspector is counting the paper clips on your desk against the inventory list. Three are missing. Explain?
left: Invent a story about the stapler

text: 7:30 p.m. The deadline was 6:00, but nobody has asked about the task. Maybe everyone forgot? Send it now, or quietly wait until morning?
You built the perfect daily plan in your planner app. It took the entire hour you’d allotted for the first task on the plan. Start, or tweak the plan?
HR announces the “Friday Hugs” initiative: every employee must hug three coworkers and log it in a form. Today is Friday.
right: Fill in the form, skip the hugs

text: The office is almost empty. The water cooler suddenly gurgles three times, though no one’s using it. The guard says that’s “the night watchman from the ’90s saying hi.”
Vadim has burned out and decided to “start a new life” today: he’s giving away his cacti and staplers. He offers you his project to maintain.
Half an hour until the presentation. The company template ate all the fonts, and the headings now look like an old greeting card. Redo it?
left: Redo it in half an hour

text: Your calendar shows three meetings at 10:00, all marked “mandatory.” Where do you go?
9:40 p.m. You’re in bed, mentally replaying yesterday’s conversation with the boss. Your inner voice offers five more versions of your comeback.
right: Put on rain sounds and sleep

text: New initiative on the portal: every employee writes an essay, “My Role in the Company’s Mission.” 3,000 characters minimum. Due Friday.
The cleaner whispers that last night the printer in the director’s office turned on by itself and printed blank pages. She’s brought you the stack.
left: Keep the pages, just in case

text: Evening English lesson in the app. The owl warns your 200-day streak will die in 15 minutes. You’re falling asleep on your feet.
The boss asks for “one small table” for the board meeting. The small table turns out to be 14 columns, 3 years of data, and a five-year forecast.
7:10 a.m. You woke up with an idea for a course: “How to Stop Procrastinating.” Start writing now, or after you hit snooze?
A poll lands in the team chat: “Are you experiencing burnout? Yes/No.” For some reason, “No” is preselected. Vote honestly?
You finish the quarterly report and hit “Save.” The program replies: “The file has been modified by another user.” There is no other user.
Management introduces a “quiet hour”: no talking from 10 to 11. At 10:15 you have an urgent question for your desk neighbor. Pass a note?
Liza writes: “Can I ask a dumb question?” — and vanishes. Forty minutes have passed. You’ve already imagined twelve possible questions.
The time tracker wants you to log how you spent the day. From memory: two hours on email, one hour looking for a file, and five hours of “other.” What do you log?
The office manager hung a “Days Until Project Launch” calendar in the elevator. The number changes every morning — sometimes upward.
The client sends feedback on the mockup: “Everything’s great, but let’s do it completely differently.” Same deadline — tomorrow at nine.
Mom calls to ask why you’re at work so late. You explain the deadline; she suggests you “just ask for one more day.” From the boss.
The quarterly plan calls for “increasing employee engagement by 30%.” Nobody knows how to measure it. You’ve been put in charge.
right: Ask who came up with this

text: The department AC only turns on when you leave the room. The moment you come back, it shuts off. Third day in a row.
The development team launches a “30 Days Without Complaining” challenge. Every offender drops a coin in a jar. Eight of the coins are already yours.
7:50 p.m. You’re alone in the office, and somewhere in Sales a phone keeps ringing. Sales left at five. Pick up?
Your desk neighbor is writing tomorrow’s to-do list. He’s moving over today’s tasks, which he moved from yesterday, which he moved from Monday.
The boss is back from a leadership training and insists on being called not “boss” but “chief inspirer.” So far, everyone is silent.
You spent the whole day watching videos about how to stop procrastinating. Zero progress on work. Your conscience asks if you’ll be working tonight, then.
A corporate values committee has been formed. Value #1: “Simplicity.” The document describing it is 46 pages long. You’re asked to sign off.
You find last year’s paper planner. On the first page: “This year I’m definitely taking up running.” The rest is blank.
left: Go for a run at lunch
right: Gift the planner to a coworker

text: 8:10 p.m. The broken printer in the corner, unplugged a month ago, prints a page reading “Report accepted.” Whose report, it doesn’t say.
The scrum master asks you to estimate a task in story points. You say 3, everyone else says 13. The task is changing one comma.
HR sends a 120-question survey: “How can we make surveys shorter?” Mandatory, due before lunch.
A coworker sent a spreadsheet with data highlighted in 14 colors and no legend. Green probably means “good.” Or “money.” Or “grass.”
You’ve already closed your laptop. Your inner voice whispers: “What if you didn’t hit Send?” Checking will cost five minutes and your peace of mind.
The intern’s first question: where can he find the policy on policies? You realize, to your surprise, that such a document really exists.
The CEO declares an open-door day: anyone can drop by with an idea. There’s a line of three at his door, all with slide decks.
left: Join the line with your idea

text: A time-management course requires watching a 40-minute lecture. There’s a “2× speed” button. There’s also a “3×” button.
The guard at the entrance asks to see not your pass but your “motivation for today.” He says it’s a new directive and hands you a form.
500 stickers reading “I can do it!” arrived at the supply room. Distribution is mandatory, five per employee, to be stuck somewhere visible.
9:00 p.m. An email marked “URGENT!!!” arrives from a department that hasn’t written to you once in two years. No subject. Open it?
That pigeon from the meeting room has learned to open the door. Now it attends stand-ups and sits in the CFO’s chair. The CFO is on vacation.
right: Let the pigeon keep the seat

text: The poster in the hallway fell, revealing an ancient one underneath: “Five-Year Plan in Three Years!” The whole team has gathered around. Put the new one back?
“Find the Leader Within,” lesson seven: “Stand in front of a mirror and say three times: ‘I am in control of my time.’” It’s 10:30 p.m.
