The boss wants “a short five-slide presentation” by lunch. The email ends with: “And attach a fifteen-slide version too, just in case.”
You walk into the meeting room and a meeting is already underway. You don’t know anyone there; they’re discussing your project and confidently getting it wrong.
You spent three hours building a formula that calculates everything automatically. Turns out the next tab has had a column with the answer all along.
The company now has a Chief Happiness Officer. He walks the rows asking everyone: “On a scale of 1 to 10, how happy are you?”
The weekly progress report is due by 10:00. The main thing you did this week was write last week’s progress report.
Sonya is heading home and says: “I’m burned out too, but in a positive way.” She suggests signing up for a ceramics class together.
The open-plan office now has “mood zones”: red means do not disturb, green means open to chat. The only free seat is in the green zone.
The coffee machine’s screen asks: “Are you sure you need coffee?” The only buttons are “Yes” and “Think it over.”
At 11:00 p.m., your inner voice suggests reevaluating your life and drawing up a five-year plan. Stand-up is at nine tomorrow.
The lawyer asks you to sign consent to the processing of your consent to data processing. It’s the third page in the stack.
You turn on your laptop and find an email from yourself, sent a year ago on a timer: “If you’re reading this, you’re still here.”
7:15 p.m. The office ficus nobody has watered in six months grew a foot and a half in one day. Today you saw it turn toward your desk.
The boss writes: “Pop by for a minute, we need to talk.” No emoji, no context. Three hours of uncertainty left in the workday.
A meeting about reducing the number of meetings. Agenda: draw up a schedule of meetings on reducing meetings. You’re asked to take minutes.
Gosha built a dashboard where every chart goes up. You notice the axes are flipped. The presentation to leadership is in fifteen minutes.
A free webinar promises “the secret of eternal energy.” Forty minutes in, it turns out the secret costs $499 in easy installments.
Accounting whispers that everyone who sat at the desk by the pillar got promoted within a month. The desk is free. Move?
The monthly sales target was hit on the 1st: a client accidentally paid an invoice twice. Management suggests “raising the bar.”
Friday night. You realize you’ve been staring at the “Shut down” button for ten minutes and can’t remember why you came to the computer.
Surprise fire safety inspection. You’re asked to show where the fire extinguisher is. You distinctly remember someone’s cactus sitting on it.
left: Move the cactus and show it

text: A flash mob in the team chat this morning: everyone’s posting photos of their breakfast. Yours is cold tea and half a cookie.
The quarterly report is almost done, but revenue is off by exactly one cent. You’ve been hunting for it for two hours.
The company hired a coach. He asks for your biggest dream “not related to work.” You say “a good night’s sleep,” and he writes it down.
Right before an important call, your laptop decided to update: “73 minutes remaining.” The call is in five. Your phone is at 4%.
8:30 p.m. In the empty office, you hear someone flipping slides in the meeting room. Lights off, nobody inside. On the screen: your presentation.
left: Go in and watch the rest

text: The project manager drew a Gantt chart where your task starts before it ends. He insists it’s “aggressive planning.”
New rewards program: for every 100 hours of overtime, you get a “Hero Employee” certificate. Printed on regular copy paper.
Tomorrow’s to-do list turned out longer than today’s. And you haven’t started today’s. What do you do with it?
You decided to eat lunch without your phone, as mindfulness courses recommend. Ten minutes in, you’re convinced the world has collapsed without you.
The HR bot sends a reminder: “Don’t forget to smile at your coworkers today. Your friendliness index is down 4%.” How does it know?
Your neighbor from the country house calls at 7:00 p.m.: she read that office workers need to “get grounded.” She invites you to dig potatoes this weekend.
Management decided the desks should be arranged in a circle, “like the Knights of the Round Table.” Your desk now has its back to the boss’s door.
The elevator stops on every floor, though no one pressed any buttons. On the 13th, the doors open onto darkness. The building has 12 floors.
At 6:30 p.m., intern Pasha asks if he can go home. He thought the workday lasts until the boss leaves. The boss sleeps at the office.
right: Say: “Hang in there, I’m here too”

text: 2:20 p.m. Your inner voice whispers that there’s still a chance to do something useful today. Your lunch insists on a siesta.
Procurement bought new “ergonomic” chairs — without backrests. They explain it strengthens your back muscles. Yours is already at your desk.
The company newsletter wants you to write a column: “How I Found Work-Life Balance.” Due tonight by midnight.
Someone secretly added a row to the shared planning sheet: “Remember why we’re doing all this.” Owner: you. Due: yesterday.
The thermos you left at the office a month ago is still hot. Inside is coffee you never poured.
Your copywriting course homework is to “sell emptiness.” Somehow you end up writing about your workday. Submit it?
Finance asks you to justify a $1 pen expense. The justification must be on official letterhead, which costs $2 a sheet.
The team lead opens stand-up with: “Let’s keep it informal today.” A minute later he shares a spreadsheet with 87 agenda items.
A neighbor asks what you do for a living. You honestly start explaining, and five minutes in you no longer understand it yourself.
The flip chart still has a note from the last strategy session: “In one year, we’ll be market leaders!” Dated three years ago.
Indoor shoes are now mandatory “for cleanliness and a homey feel.” You’re in a meeting with the director wearing bunny slippers.
right: Hide your feet under the table

text: Your email client sends a report: “This week you sent 312 emails, spent 22 hours in meetings, and worked for 3 hours.” Share it with the boss?
Olya suggests trying the Pomodoro technique together: 25 minutes of work, 5 of rest. By the third pomodoro you’re discussing vacations.
A courier delivers a package to the office in your name. Inside: a box of chocolates and a note: “Hang in there till Friday. A well-wisher.”
The strategy session is in its sixth hour. The facilitator proposes “one last exercise”: draw the company as an animal.
The boss is back from a conference and announces the team will now work “like a startup”: desks are gone, everyone sits on beanbags. Yours is shaped like a pear.
The meeting room pigeon laid an egg right in the paper tray. The printer now prints around the nest. Facilities wants a decision by tonight.
On the subway, your inner voice suggests quitting, moving to the beach, and selling corn on the cob. It does this every Tuesday.
Analytics found that the most productive employees arrive by 7:00 a.m. Starting next week, everyone is invited to “voluntarily” come in at seven.
You’re presenting, and on slide seven you find a note: “joke here.” There’s no joke. Everyone’s waiting.
Your meditation app reminds you: “You haven’t meditated in 47 days. We’re worried.” Even the app is anxious on your behalf.
A committee from headquarters is checking “workflow hygiene.” They want to know why you have 34 tabs open.
right: Close all tabs in front of them

text: The poster by the elevator reads: “Dream! Act! Achieve!” This morning someone covered up “Act” and “Achieve.” Only “Dream!” remains.
right: Do some dreaming by the elevator

text: At 6:05 p.m., the boss asks for the report “in the format we discussed.” You didn’t discuss anything. Maybe in a past life.
The director’s assistant wants a “clear project summary” from you in an hour. The project is three years old, and no one remembers what it’s about.
Accounting issued a new business-trip report form. It’s 9 pages, two of which are instructions on how to fill out the instructions.
At 7:40 p.m., you find a sticky note on your desk in your own handwriting: “Don’t forget about Thursday.” You didn’t write it. Today is Thursday.
The project office introduced traffic-light statuses. Your project has been yellow for six months: not green, but not red enough to shut down.
9:30 a.m. Fifty people are editing a shared spreadsheet at once. Someone is erasing your numbers, and their cursor is labeled “Anonymous Raccoon.”
A friend invites you to yoga, where the instructor promises to “free you from work thoughts.” Half an hour in, you’re in “report-due-by-morning” pose.
Igor is back from a public speaking course and now opens every chat message with a pause and a dramatic “Friends…”
right: Ask him to keep it short

text: Your phone alarm now has a label: “Time to rise, report hero.” You didn’t write that. Looks like someone got hold of your phone at the office party.
You set a 25-minute work timer. It went off, and all you managed was finding the right file. Set another, or go home?
The CEO suddenly walks into the department: “What are you working on right now?” Your screen shows the 2028 vacation schedule.
Marketing announced the new company logo is a “spiral of growth.” Employees see a snail. You’re asked to send it to clients.
9:15 p.m. An email from the boss with a single word: “Well?” You have no idea what it’s about. There were no new tasks.
You’ve been enrolled in “Advanced Excel.” Lesson one: “How to Find the Save Button.” 39 lessons to go.
Security is running a test: everyone got a planted USB stick labeled “Everyone’s salaries.” Yours is sitting on your keyboard. Oh, the temptation.
right: Hold it and put it down

text: Your conscience reminds you that you promised to check a coworker’s report back on Monday. It’s now Friday evening, and he’s already sent it himself.
right: Act like it was the plan

text: A cat has appeared in the office. No one knows whose it is or where it came from. Today it’s sitting on your keyboard and won’t budge.
right: Move the cat to your neighbor

text: New instructions require a 12-point checklist before every email, including “Have you considered the recipient’s feelings?”
You signed up for the webinar “How Not to Burn Out,” but it’s at the same time as your evening call. Choose between prevention and the cause.
Someone in the team chat proposed a “productivity challenge”: whoever closes the most tasks by Friday gets a cake. Everyone’s already racing.
right: Give up and wait for cake

text: Your office key now only opens the supply closet. And the supply closet key opens the director’s office. The facilities manager is on vacation.
At 7:30 p.m., the smart speaker in the meeting room announces on its own: “Reminder: meeting with you.” Nobody knows who scheduled it. Wait for the meeting?
You’re writing a document, and in the next tab someone is editing it in real time. The cursor shows it’s the boss. He’s fixing commas.
The department head introduced “Monday weekly plan reports” and “Friday unfinished plan reports.” Today is Monday.
The company’s “Healthy Back” club meets at 6:30. The instructor is an accountant who threw out his back yesterday filing reports.
Surprise check: the director is personally walking the desks asking everyone what the company’s mission is. Three people to go before you.
right: Put it in your own words

text: On the subway you see an ad for a course: “How to Quit and Be Happy.” It’s hanging right in front of your face. Again.
You’ve stayed late and notice the paper clips on your desk have arranged themselves into a shape. It looks like a sales chart. It’s going down.
New policy: every coffee break must be requested through the system. Approval arrives in 40 minutes.
Since morning, Sveta has been handing out daily affirmations on slips of paper. You got: “I am a strong, independent spreadsheet.”
Your phone shows your weekly screen time: 42 hours in the work chat. That’s more than you slept. What do you do?
You sit down for lunch, and the cafeteria starts playing an hour-long video of the CEO’s speech. Volume at max.
The office clock stopped at 9:00 six months ago. New hires think it’s always morning here and show up at lunchtime. Fix it?
The project you fought for over six months was shut down “for strategic reasons.” Announced at 6:45 p.m. with one word in chat: “Wrapping up.”
The mandatory efficiency training lasts six hours. Module one: “How Not to Waste Time on Useless Things.”
right: Work on your laptop in training

text: Your inner voice declares that today is the day you start getting up at six. It’s 8:47, and you’re late.
Your fitness band reports you walked 412 steps today and survived 14 stress episodes. It suggests some breathing.
A “Paperless Office” initiative is announced. To participate, print and sign the application in triplicate.
The Chief Innovation Officer wants to replace stand-ups with a “stand-up comedy show”: everyone reports their tasks with a joke. You’re up next.
Every evening at 6:13, the department lights go out for exactly one second. Old-timers say you should announce “I’m leaving” out loud at that moment.
For the sixth time on the call, the client asks if it can be “a little brighter, but more understated.” He sincerely awaits an answer.
7:20 p.m. A courier delivers a huge “Employee of the Month” certificate. Your first name is misspelled, and the last name belongs to someone else.
right: Send it back to be redone

text: At 6:01 p.m., your inner voice asks: “How about a little more work, since we’re here anyway?” It said that yesterday too, and you left at ten.
The boss comes up with a “Friday innovation hour”: every employee must propose one revolutionary idea. It’s Wednesday, but the hour is already booked.
Today the meeting room pigeon spoke for the first time. Or rather, it made a sound exactly like your messenger’s incoming call. You’ve jumped up three times.
HR sends an evening survey: “How burned out are you, on a scale from ‘a little’ to ‘ashes’?” Anonymity guaranteed — but there’s a “Full name” field.
The spreadsheet refuses to sort alphabetically. Names starting with Ö land at the very end, and there’s just one: a lonely employee named Öberg.
Friday morning, you find out that the report you’ve been submitting all month was never read by anyone. It was archived automatically.
An evening online coding course. The task: print “Hello, World.” All you can print is a 200-line error.
Security sends a notice: your password is too weak. The new password must contain a letter, a number, a hieroglyph, and an emotion.
right: Write it on a sticky note

text: The morning meeting has been going for forty minutes. You suddenly realize no one has ever said what it’s about. Everyone’s nodding.
Every night, the same diagram appears on the meeting room whiteboard. It’s erased in the morning; by evening it’s back. Today you’ve decided to stay and watch.
The head of business development asks you to record a short video, “Why I Love My Job,” for the careers site. Three takes have already flopped.
Your calendar reminds you: “Prepare for tomorrow’s meeting prep.” You scheduled it yourself. When?
You’re listening to “The Power of Morning” on the way home. The host urges you to get up at five and write three pages of thoughts. You’re on episode 22.
The company library loaned you the book “How to Say No.” It must be returned at any coworker’s request. Three have already asked.
right: Give it to the first one

text: The office manager hung a “No Whining Today” sign and set out a fine jar. It’s 9:15, and two of the coins are already yours.
A quarterly review has been scheduled for Friday evening “in an informal setting.” Informal means pizza and a scorecard for each person.
All day, your desk neighbor loudly repeats a mantra from a course: “I am calm, I am focused.” Which makes it impossible for you to focus.
left: Ask him to keep it down

text: The commuter train has stopped in the middle of a field. The driver announced a “technical break.” You watch the cows and realize it’s the best morning in a month.
Your inner critic rereads the email you sent a client at 4:00 p.m. It finds three typos and one misplaced parenthesis.
The time-management course assignment: log your day for forty minutes. Twenty of them went to finding a pen.
Poster in the kitchen: “We’re a family!” Next to it, a note: “Whoever ate my yogurt is not family.” The whole team recognizes the handwriting.
Mom says she dreamed you were swamped at work. She’s right. She also asks why you never call. It’s 8:15 p.m.
The CFO wants the department to cut expenses by 10%. The biggest expense is his own subscription to an analytics journal.
All your cards on the task board have moved to the “Done” column. You didn’t finish anything. Someone clearly wishes you well. Or ill.
You finally filled in the vacation spreadsheet. At 6:30 p.m., an email arrives: “We’ve switched to a new system, please move everything there.”
The productivity guru invited to lead the training is forty minutes late. He explains he was working on higher-priority tasks.
Dima announced he now lives by the rule “Never do today what you can delegate.” He’s already delegated three tasks to you.
You try to shut down your laptop, and it asks: “Save changes to 17 files?” You don’t remember a single one of them.
Management launches a survey: “What should the ideal corporate culture look like?” The options: “Like now” and “Like now, but better.”
The entrance turnstile displays: “Access restricted. Reason: low motivation.” The guard shrugs and suggests some deep breathing.
At 6:20 p.m., Sales invites you “for a minute” to celebrate closing a deal. Their minutes usually last until the last train.
The CEO writes in an all-staff email: “Our people are our greatest asset.” The next email announces a bonus freeze.
At 8:20 a.m., the person next to you on the subway is reading “How to Do Nothing and Get Everything Done.” You can only see the cover. You’re dying to ask if it works.
right: Snap a photo of the cover

text: You stayed until 7:30 p.m., and the meeting room pigeon is still there. It gives you an understanding look: it never goes home either.
right: Turn off the lights and leave

text: The company English course requires speaking only English in meetings. Your vocabulary: “okay,” “deadline,” and “sync.”
Management decided to fight burnout with “No-Call Wednesdays.” It’s Wednesday, and you’ve been invited to three “quick non-calls.”
Your conscience reminds you that you meant to hit the gym today. The membership was bought in January, it’s now October, and you lost your locker key.
The report is perfect except for one thing: the total line says “roughly this much” instead of a number. It was sent directly to the CEO.
The executive assistant books you into a meeting: “Discussion of item 4.” You don’t have items 1–3. The meeting is in ten minutes.
right: Postpone until you get the items

text: You’re falling asleep when your inner voice whispers: “Are you sure you turned off the coffee machine?” You never turn on the coffee machine. You drink tea.
The workplace safety engineer is checking your chair height. It’s an inch above regulation. You’ve been sitting in it for three years.
The Monday morning meeting is set for 8:00 a.m. “to set the pace for the week.” You’ll be setting the pace with your eyes closed.
You ordered a yoga mat, but the courier also brought the book “How to Stop Buying Self-Improvement Stuff.” Billed to you.
HR promises: whoever completes 50 courses on the company portal gets a “Lifelong Learner” badge and a mug. You have 48 to go.
Intern Ksyusha accidentally posted her plan “How I’ll Survive This Week” in the group chat. Item 3 has your name: “Avoid at all costs.”
8:05 p.m. The portal published a ranking of the “Most Active Employees.” You’re number one because you forgot to log out over the weekend.
right: Ask them to fix the ranking

text: Nobody has worked in room 404 for a year. Yet every day someone drinks coffee there: there’s a fresh mug on the desk. Today it has your name on it.
You signed up for an art class to unwind from work. Lesson one: “Draw your dream.” You drew a pie chart.
Someone invented a spreadsheet for tracking spreadsheets. You have to log all of yours. You have 63, and half are called “New.”
The cleaner locked you in the office, thinking everyone had left. No key, phone at 5%, and there’s leftover pizza in the kitchen from yesterday’s party.
The boss opens the day with: “I have a challenge for you!” The challenge: prepare the annual plan in one day while he’s at a conference.
right: Ask for at least a week

text: The meeting room pigeon has been added to the org chart as “team mascot.” Now it needs a badge. You’re taking the photo.
7:10 p.m. Your inner voice suggests buying the course “How to Stop Buying Courses.” The 70% discount expires at midnight.
The company switched to a new task system. To create a task, you first have to create a task called “Create task.” You have 30 tasks.
right: Keep a list in a notebook

text: The motivation committee installed a gong in the department. Anyone who closes a task must strike it. Your neighbors bang it every five minutes.
The report is ready, but the boss asks you to “give it a bit more air.” You’ve already spaced out the lines and enlarged the margins and font. Still not airy enough.
New poster in the department: “Success is 1% talent and 99% overtime.” The team has already recalculated their pay accordingly.
A surprise inspection from headquarters wants to see “a business process in action.” Everyone freezes and pretends to work. Except you — you were eating.
Your roommate asks why you’re talking to your laptop at 9:00 p.m. You explain it was a rehearsal for tomorrow’s presentation.
right: Give up and watch a show

text: Since this morning, the reception shredder has refused to shred. It spits documents back out, neatly folded. They’re your documents.
You hit a button by accident, and the spreadsheet sorted employees by burnout level. Someone hid that column long ago. You’re number one.
Evening driving lessons. The instructor asks why you check work email at red lights. He’s seen it three times now.
The elevator mirror says: “Smile, you’re doing great!” Today, for the first time this week, you smile. The elevator instantly gets stuck between floors.
The HR director is hosting an “open hearts hour”: everyone must share their biggest fear at work.
right: Talk about fear of being late

text: You’ve been staring at the wall for twenty minutes and calling it “strategic thinking.” A coworker asks what you’re thinking about.
9:00 a.m. The organizer of the morning meeting is late. Six people sit in silence. Someone quietly starts eating an apple, and everyone can hear it.
The portal awarded you a “Deadline Master” medal for submitting a report one minute before it was due. Your boss got the same one.
left: Put the medal on your avatar

text: You find a draft email you wrote six months ago: “I’m leaving, thanks everyone.” Never sent. What do you do with it?
The receptionist puts a jar on the counter labeled “For good ideas.” Inside: three ideas and some loose change. Add yours?
Every day at 2:00 p.m., someone leaves the same newspaper from 1998 in the kitchen. Today its crossword is filled in — in your handwriting.
At your evening financial literacy class, you’re asked to calculate your hourly rate. Counting overtime, it’s less than a delivery courier’s.
The intern’s first question: “Are you actually happy here? It’s for my term paper.” The phone camera is already rolling.
The internal idea accelerator accepted your idea: “Cut half of all reports.” You’ve been put in charge of preparing a report on it.
At 11:40 p.m., your inner voice suddenly remembers you promised to reply to a coworker “by tonight.” Technically, it’s still tonight.
At 7:30 a.m., someone posted a six-minute voice message in the team chat. It begins: “So, real quick.” Listen before stand-up?
The shift supervisor created a “wall of shame and fame.” Your photo is hung in the middle, since they couldn’t decide on your category.
The deadline was moved to Monday. Which means the weekend is now officially a workday — unofficially.
Marketing wants all employees to switch their profile pics to branded ones with the logo and a smile. The photographer arrives at 11:00.
The client asks if it’s possible to “put a timer on user happiness.” You’re not sure what that is, but he’s ready to pay.
8:40 p.m. The night watchman tells you the office was built where an alarm clock factory used to be. That, he says, is why everyone here is so tired.
The company launches a “Bike to Work” campaign. Cyclists get a bonus. Your bike’s tires went flat last season.
The business coach suggests stepping out of your comfort zone: sing the team anthem. There is no anthem — you have five minutes to write one.
A courier delivers pizza to the department “for the overtime crew.” The boss ordered it, then left. The box says: “For heroes.”
Someone wrote on the restroom mirror in marker: “You’ve got this.” Today, for the first time, you believed it. Who’s writing these?
At stand-up, they decided to make a “wall of achievements.” Everyone posts their biggest win of the month. Yours: you didn’t cry once.
Tonya is leaving and puts a note on your desk: “Don’t stay late, it’s contagious.” You were already thinking of staying.
The new robot cleaner has chosen your desk as its base. Every morning it bumps your leg and drives off. Today — twice.
Supply replaced all the paper with eco-paper. It’s gray and rough, and the printer won’t take it. Report due at 3:00.
left: Feed it one sheet at a time

text: A self-improvement course sent you a certificate of completion. You didn’t take a single lesson. The system must have decided you’re improved enough.
At 9:05 a.m., auditors arrive and ask to see “the log of logs.” This is the first you’ve heard such a log exists.
left: Start a log in front of them

text: At 3:30 p.m., your inner voice announces: “You’ve done enough work today.” This morning’s task is still marked “New.”
You’re eating at a restaurant for the first time in a month. The waiter asks if you’re comfortable, since you’ve reflexively opened your laptop on the table.
Misha shares that he’s adopted a new system: every morning he writes three pages of thoughts. Today all three are about you.
Only one fish is left in the lobby aquarium. Rumor has it she didn’t get a raise either. Today she’s swimming circles faster than usual.
Your inner voice asks if it’s finally time to clean up your computer desktop. There are 214 files named “Screenshot.”
The weekly task sheet shows 112% capacity. The boss asks you to add one more “to make it 120%, it looks nicer.”
The office cactus you promised to water yesterday has dried up. Next to it is a note from your neighbor: “Wow. Just wow.”
At 7:30 p.m., a company-wide email arrives: “Starting Monday, the dress code is ‘Inspiration.’” No further details.
right: Show up tomorrow in a scarf

text: You’re riding your scooter home when you realize you forgot to save the report. The office is five minutes back. Turn around?
Friday evening, a message appears on your monitor: “You survived. See you Monday.” The computer was off.
